android.prompt_ui: Automatic sign in with a one time consent; manual sign in button
android.revocation: Play Games app > Settings > Delete Play Games account
android.store_policy: Play: PGS v2 required for new releases
android.api_surface: Play Games Services v2 GamesSignInClient, PlayersClient, Saved Games
android.note: PGS v1 is retired; Play Games on PC uses the same account.

ios.prompt_ui: Game Center banner; sign in to Apple ID
ios.note: iOS 26 adds a Games app with challenges and Activity feed.

limits.headline: Can sign you in to your game account to save progress and post scores
limits.user_action: You open a game and tap Sign in, or it signs you in on first launch
can: Sign you in to Play Games or Game Center with the account already on the phone
Show your player name and profile picture in the game
Save game progress to the platform's cloud
Post scores and unlock achievements
cannot: See your Google or Apple account password
See your friends list without your approval
Move progress to the other platform (iPhone to Android or back)
Sign you in when you decline or turn the service off
limits.differs: Android uses Play Games Services and signs in automatically. iPhone uses Game Center and shows a sign in prompt.

story.what_it_is: You sign into the phone's built in game account, so scores, saves and friends follow you.

marketing.name: Google Play Games services
marketing.pitch: One game profile that carries your achievements, cloud saves and leaderboards across devices.

marketing.name: Game Center
marketing.pitch: Apple's social gaming network for friends, leaderboards and achievements across your Apple devices.

story.for_you: When you open a game you see a small welcome banner with your gamer name. Your progress is saved to the account and shows up on a new phone. Friends can see your scores and invite you to play.
story.for_makers: Makers get a ready made player ID, friends list, leaderboard and cloud save without building their own. It also gives the platform a link between your play in many games, which helps with recommendations and retention.

use_cases.example: A puzzle game restores your levels and coins on a new phone after you sign in with your game account.
A racing game shows your lap time against friends on a leaderboard.
A multiplayer game uses your friends list to start a match or invite someone straight into your party.
An AR title saves your collection to the game account so a lost phone does not wipe it.
A kids game uses an account managed by a parent so achievements are saved without a new password.
A studio sees returning players across devices and counts a person once, not three phones.

story.android_note: Android uses Play Games, and it signs in automatically when the player has a Google account on the phone.
story.ios_note: iPhone uses Game Center, and the player signs in once in Settings and can turn it off per app.

technical_bounds: Friends list needs player consent

history.change: Automatic sign in replaces explicit sign in

capabilities.name: Hardware backed keys (Keystore and Secure Enclave)
capabilities.plain: Creates cryptographic keys that never leave the phone's secure chip.
capabilities.meaning: A device-bound key proves that a request comes from one specific phone. The iOS Keychain can survive app deletion, which lets services recognise a returning device.

android.prompt_ui: Key is deleted on app uninstall; user auth binding optional
android.api_surface: KeyGenParameterSpec, StrongBox (API 28), setUserAuthenticationRequired, key attestation, Play Integrity
android.note: Hardware attestation certificates prove device model and OS patch level.

ios.revocation: Delete data via Settings; erase device
ios.api_surface: Keychain Services, kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave, SecAccessControl .biometryCurrentSet, App Attest
ios.note: Items without a data protection class limit survive reinstall; Secure Enclave keys are only P-256.

limits.headline: Can make secret keys that stay locked inside your phone's security chip
limits.user_action: Nothing, or you confirm with fingerprint or face when the app sets up secure sign in
can: Create a key in the phone's secure chip
Sign data or log in with that key without exposing it
Require your fingerprint or face each time the key is used
Prove which phone model and security patch level it is on (Android)
cannot: Take the key out of the chip or copy it to a server
Use the key after you remove the screen lock, when set to require one
Use other key types in the iPhone Secure Enclave; it only supports P-256
Move the key to a new phone
limits.reach_label: Keys only usable on this phone
limits.differs: Android can prove the model and patch level. iPhone Secure Enclave keys are limited to one key type and are checked by Face ID or Touch ID.

story.what_it_is: An app makes a secret key that is stored in a locked chip and never leaves your phone.

marketing.name: Android Keystore
marketing.pitch: Keys live in protected hardware so even malware cannot copy them out of the phone.

marketing.name: Secure Enclave
marketing.pitch: A separate chip that holds keys and checks Face ID or Touch ID without sharing them with the app.

story.for_you: You never see the key. What you notice is smooth, safe actions like approving a payment with a face scan, and a login that does not need a password. The secret stays on the phone.
story.for_makers: Makers can prove that a login or payment came from one specific phone, which is strong protection against stolen passwords. The key can also tie an account to a device, and on iPhone some keychain items survive an uninstall, which helps services recognize a returning phone.

use_cases.example: A bank signs each money transfer with a hardware key so a stolen password alone cannot move funds.
A wallet app approves a tap to pay with a key that only unlocks after you scan your face.
A game uses a device key to sign purchase requests and block fake receipts.
A company ties staff logins to company phones with keys, so a copied password is useless on another device.
A cryptocurrency app keeps its signing key inside the chip so malware cannot read it.
A digital car key stores a key in the chip so your phone can unlock and start the car.

story.android_note: Android may keep keys in the main secure chip or a separate StrongBox chip, depending on the phone model.
story.ios_note: iPhone keychain items can survive deleting an app, so a service may still recognise a returning phone.

technical_bounds: Key material is never extractable

refs.label: Apple: Protecting keys with the Secure Enclave

capabilities.name: Identifier for Vendor (IDFV)
capabilities.plain: A per-vendor iOS ID that is the same across one developer's apps.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a developer link their own apps on one phone with no prompt. Resets when the last app by that vendor is deleted.

android.note: Closest analog is Android ID

ios.revocation: App Review: not for ads or cross-vendor tracking
ios.api_surface: UUID; may be nil before first unlock after restart; resets when all vendor apps are removed
ios.note: Until all apps from the vendor are deleted

limits.headline: Can recognize you across apps from the same developer on iPhone, but not other developers
limits.user_action: Nothing. Any app can ask for it as soon as it opens
can: Use one shared ID across all of one developer's apps on your iPhone
Count how many different people use the developer's apps
Keep the same ID until every app from that developer is deleted
cannot: Match you to apps from other developers; each developer gets a different ID
Exist on Android; there is no direct match, only Android ID
Stay the same after you delete all of that developer's apps
Be available before your first unlock after a restart
limits.differs: This exists only on iPhone. Android has a similar but different ID (Android ID).

story.what_it_is: An iOS ID that is the same for all apps from one developer on your phone.

marketing.name: identifierForVendor
marketing.pitch: Developer pitch: an alphanumeric string that identifies the device to the app's vendor, shared by that vendor's apps.

story.for_you: You never see it and no pop up appears. It lets one company, like a game studio with several games, know the same phone runs all its apps. It resets when you delete the last app from that company.
story.for_makers: Makers can link their own apps on one phone with no prompt and without Apple's tracking rules. It helps with saving progress, fraud checks and cross promotion between their own titles.

use_cases.example: A studio that makes five puzzle games sees that the same phone plays all of them and offers a bonus in the new game.
A streaming company uses it to hide its trial offer from a phone that already used it in a sister app.
A publisher builds an audience of people who play several of its own apps and sells ads to that group.
A developer joins crash logs from three of its apps to see that one phone is failing everywhere.
A bank app group spots many accounts that share one vendor ID and applies stricter checks.
A retailer with a store app and a coupon app knows both are on the same phone and syncs your points.

story.android_note: Android has no matching ID, so this does not exist there.
story.ios_note: Free to read with no prompt and it is not limited by the Ask App Not to Track choice because it stays inside one company.

technical_bounds: Scoped to one vendor

capabilities.name: Passkeys in an app (create and sign in)
capabilities.plain: Creates and uses phishing resistant passkeys for sign in inside an app.
capabilities.meaning: Replaces passwords with device-held keys; an app learns only a public key, never the biometric. Passkeys sync through the platform keychain, so account recovery shifts to Google or Apple.

android.permission: None (Credential Manager API 34; Jetpack back to Android 4.4 with Play services passkeys on 9+)
android.prompt_ui: Bottom sheet: Create passkey / Use saved passkey with biometric confirm
android.persistence: Syncs across devices through Google Password Manager
android.revocation: Settings > Passwords & accounts > Google Password Manager
android.note: Digital Asset Links bind app and domain (assetlinks.json); Android 14 adds credential provider support.

ios.prompt_ui: Sheet with passkey and Face ID or Touch ID confirm
ios.note: iOS 17 adds passkey manager providers and conditional UI; iOS 26 adds passkey import and export between providers.

limits.headline: Can create and use passkeys inside the app after you approve with your device lock
limits.user_action: You tap Create a passkey or Sign in with a passkey, then confirm with fingerprint, face or PIN
can: Create a passkey for your account tied to the app and its website
Sign you in with a passkey instead of a password
Show a system sheet listing the passkeys you already have
Sync passkeys through your password manager or cloud keychain
cannot: See your private passkey or your screen lock
Use a passkey without your approval each time
Use the passkey on a different website or app than it was made for
Work on very old phones without Google Play services (Android)
limits.reach_label: One approved sign in at a time
limits.differs: Android uses Credential Manager. iPhone needs the app tied to its website and supports other managers from iOS 17.

story.what_it_is: You sign in with a face or fingerprint scan instead of a password.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: Sign in with Face ID or Touch ID instead of passwords, and passkeys sync across your Apple devices.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: Android and Google make passkeys the simple, safer way to sign in without remembering passwords.

story.for_you: You tap sign in, glance at your phone or touch the sensor, and you are in. No password to remember or type. A fake site cannot steal it because the passkey only works on the real one.
story.for_makers: Makers see fewer password resets, fewer stolen accounts and quicker sign ups. It also moves the key storage to Apple or Google, so recovery and lock in become the platform's problem and power.

use_cases.example: A shop lets you create a passkey after your first order, then logs you in next time with a face scan.
A bank swaps password and text code for a passkey, which cuts phishing losses.
A game platform signs you in with a passkey so a hacked reused password cannot steal your skins.
A social app lets you sign in with a passkey from your tablet through the shared keychain.
An airline app signs you in with a passkey, so you check in fast at the airport.
A company login uses passkeys so staff stop falling for fake login pages.

risks: Recovery depends on Google or Apple
story.android_note: Android stores passkeys in Google Password Manager or a chosen provider and syncs them to your other Android devices.
story.ios_note: iPhone stores passkeys in iCloud Keychain, and since iOS 17 other apps can offer to hold them too.

technical_bounds: Both vendors sync keys with their own cloud

capabilities.name: Play Integrity verdicts
capabilities.plain: Google returns a signed verdict on the device, app, and account integrity.
capabilities.meaning: Verdict levels (BASIC, DEVICE, STRONG) tell servers if a phone is rooted, an emulator, or running an altered app. STRONG (Android 13+) needs hardware-backed signals and a recent patch.

android.store_policy: Play policy
android.note: MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY, MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY, MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY; STRONG needs a security patch within the last 12 months

ios.note: See App Attest entry

limits.headline: Can ask Google whether the phone and app look genuine and unmodified
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you sign in, pay, or do something the app wants to protect
can: Ask Google for a signed verdict on the device, the app, and the Play license
See whether the phone passes basic, device, or strong integrity
Block actions on rooted, emulated or tampered devices
cannot: See who you are or your Google account details
See other apps on your phone
Give a strong verdict if the security patch is older than about 12 months
Work on iPhone; App Attest does that job
limits.reach_label: A verdict about the device and app
limits.differs: Only Android has Play Integrity. iPhone uses App Attest.

story.what_it_is: Google tells a server whether the phone, the app and the account look genuine.

marketing.name: Play Integrity API
marketing.pitch: Google helps apps detect risky or fake devices and apps so they can fight fraud, cheating and abuse.

story.for_you: You never see it. It runs in the background when you log in, buy something or play online. It can make a game or bank app refuse to run on a rooted phone or a custom system.
story.for_makers: Makers get a signed answer from Google about whether the device is real, the app is untouched and it was installed from Google Play. They use it to cut cheaters, bots and card fraud. It also locks out some honest users with custom software.

use_cases.example: A shooter checks the phone before a ranked match so cheat tool users are blocked.
A bank app refuses to open on a rooted phone, because malware could read the screen.
A payments app verifies the device before it approves a high value transfer.
A sale app limits scripted bots grabbing limited stock by checking each request.
A streaming app uses it to block pirated, repackaged copies of the app.
A new sign up is checked for emulators so one person cannot create thousands of fake accounts.

story.android_note: This is the Google service for Android, and the strongest verdict needs a recent security update and hardware signals.
story.ios_note: iPhone has no version. Apps use Apple App Attest for the same job.

technical_bounds: Server-side verdict

List all accounts on your phone without you opening the picker
See your Gmail or Drive files without a separate approval

story.what_it_is: One tap signs you into an app with a Google account already on your phone.

marketing.pitch: Create an account or sign in with one tap using your Google account instead of a new password.

A delivery app pre fills your email so your first order is faster.

story.what_it_is: A long ID Android keeps for each developer's apps on one phone.

marketing.name: Android ID (SSAID)
marketing.pitch: Developer guide: a 64 bit value that is unique per app signing key and user, and resets on factory reset.

story.for_you: You never see it and it asks nothing. It lets one company recognize your phone across its apps, and it changes only if you factory reset or the developer changes signing keys.

A payments app counts how many accounts used one phone ID and blocks the tenth.
An ad attribution tool uses it to tie an install to a click when the ad ID has been turned off.
A coupon app makes sure a one time welcome offer is not redeemed again on the same phone.
A product team counts unique devices over months without asking for a login.
A company device manager uses it to know which phone is which in its fleet.

story.what_it_is: Small saved data that stays on your phone or in the cloud even after you delete the app.

marketing.name: Block Store
marketing.pitch: Developer pitch: save credentials or small data so users can restore their sign in on a new Android device.

story.for_you: After you delete and reinstall an app, it may still know who you are and sign you in without a password. You might see that as helpful. You will not see that the app also remembers things you thought were wiped.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to restore sign in after a phone upgrade and to stop abuse, like free trials claimed over and over. The same trick also lets a company recognize a returning person after a clean install.

use_cases.example: You buy a new phone and the game signs you in and brings your saved profile back with no password.
A shopping app remembers a coupon was used on this phone even after you reinstall.
A wallet app notices a reinstall by the same person and avoids sending a second verification text.
A dating or banking app spots a banned user who deleted the app and started again.
A streaming app limits a free trial to one per phone, even if you remove and add the app.
An ad firm keeps a stable ID that outlives uninstall so campaign results are not broken by reinstalls.

story.android_note: Block Store can also move data to a new phone, and Auto Backup can restore app data.
story.ios_note: Keychain items often remain after the app is deleted, and the person cannot easily see or clear them.

marketing.name: Digital ID in Google Wallet
marketing.pitch: Google Wallet can hold a digital ID, with the participating states and partners growing over time.

story.for_you: You scan the front of your ID, take a selfie and follow a few head turns. After that your license sits in your wallet. You can show it at the airport or share one fact online.
story.for_makers: Governments and wallet makers want to move ID checks from plastic to phones. Businesses benefit from signed details that are hard to fake. It also makes the phone vendor the keeper of one of the most important documents you own.

use_cases.example: You tap your phone at the airport security line instead of pulling out a plastic license.
A shop checks your age at pickup of a restricted item by reading your wallet ID.
A bank confirms who you are when you open a new account from your couch.
A car rental desk lets you skip the counter by sharing your license from your wallet.
A scammer sends a fake 'verify your ID' link, which is why real wallet requests always show a system sheet.
A building uses wallet IDs to sign in guests without paper badges.

story.what_it_is: A hardware ID used by video DRM that apps can sometimes read as a phone fingerprint.

marketing.name: Widevine DRM
marketing.pitch: Pitch: content protection that lets streaming services play licensed video safely on Android and the web.

story.for_you: You never see it. It works behind the scenes so a protected movie will play, and it may also act as a long lasting tag on your phone that survives clearing app data.
story.for_makers: Streaming services need it to give out licences and set quality levels. Because it can stay the same after a reset, some apps use it as a hard to remove device ID for fraud checks and device tracking.

use_cases.example: A streaming app checks your phone's Widevine level before allowing HD or 4K playback.
A service limits how many phones one account can download offline shows to, counting them by device ID.
A fraud team blocks an account sharing scam that signs in from the same hardware over and over.
A cloud gaming app checks that a phone has secure video decoding before it allows protected streams.
A tracker reads a value that outlives a reset to rebuild a profile after you clear your ad ID.
A live sports app uses DRM licences so a match feed cannot be recorded by ripping the stream.

risks: Hard to reset on your own
story.android_note: Newer Android versions restrict this per app, and some phones now return an app specific value.
story.ios_note: iPhone uses Apple's own FairPlay system, so this ID does not exist there.

technical_bounds: Behavior varies by OEM and version

android.note: Returns verified or supervised status and age lower and upper bounds

ios.note: Parent can approve sharing; returns bands such as 13 to 15

limits.user_action: You approve sharing your age range, or a parent approves for a child

story.what_it_is: An app asks the phone which age group you are in, without learning your birth date.

marketing.pitch: Apps can ask for an age range that a parent or user has shared, without learning exact birth dates.

marketing.name: Play Age Signals
marketing.pitch: Google gives apps an age signal to help them follow child safety laws.

story.for_you: You or a parent set your age once. An app may ask for your age group, and you may see a prompt asking whether to share it. Teens may see a more limited version of the app.
story.for_makers: New laws push app makers to protect children, and a trustworthy age signal is easier than checking IDs. The rule is that the app gets a band like 13 to 15, not a date. Getting it wrong either shuts out young users or puts them in unsafe spaces.

use_cases.example: A social app switches off direct messages from strangers for people in the teen band.
A game turns off open voice chat and loot box offers for under 13 players.
A video app picks a kids profile when the age signal says a child is watching.
A dating app keeps minors out by asking the phone for an age check instead of a typed birthday.
A store hides age restricted items from younger shoppers.
A learning app asks a parent to approve a child's account when the age band says under 13.

risks: Age band can still be shared widely
story.android_note: Android apps get an age signal through Google Play for supervised accounts and in places where laws require it.
story.ios_note: iPhone shows a prompt and the person or a parent decides whether to share a range with the app.

User or parent can decline
Law status in Texas was in court at time of writing

story.what_it_is: A server gets proof that a request came from the real app on a genuine phone.

marketing.name: App Attest
marketing.pitch: Apple lets servers confirm requests come from a genuine copy of the app on Apple hardware.

marketing.name: Play Integrity API
marketing.pitch: Google tells servers whether a device, app and account look real or risky.

story.for_you: You do not see it. It sits behind a sign up, a purchase or a score upload and quietly says 'this looks real'. If your phone is jailbroken or rooted, an app may stop working.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to block bots, cheats and cloned apps. It is a device level proof, not a person level ID, which helps with privacy. It still decides which phones are allowed and which are turned away.

use_cases.example: A game server checks that a match result came from the real game, not a modified copy.
A bank checks that a transfer request came from its real app before it moves any money.
A ticket seller blocks scripts that buy up concert seats by checking each purchase.
A social app slows fake account creation by asking new devices to prove they are real.
An ad platform removes fake installs by confirming the app and device were genuine.
An AI app protects its paid server by only answering the true app.

risks: Device key can act as an identifier
story.android_note: Android uses Play Integrity and gives a graded answer (basic, device, strong) about the device.
story.ios_note: iPhone uses App Attest, which is a hardware key per app install plus a signed statement from Apple.

technical_bounds: Server must verify; clients cannot trust local result

story.what_it_is: You sign in with your Apple account and can hide your real email address.

marketing.name: Sign in with Apple
marketing.pitch: A private, simple way to sign in with Face ID, with the option to hide your email address.

marketing.name: Credential Manager
marketing.pitch: Android's single sign in sheet for passwords, passkeys and federated sign in options.

story.for_you: You see a black Apple button, tap it and confirm with Face ID. You can pick Hide My Email, so the app gets a random address that forwards to your real inbox. You can switch it off later.
story.for_makers: Makers get a fast sign up with a verified account, which means more finished sign ups. If you hide your email, they cannot easily link you to other data. It also means the maker must send mail to the relay and cannot simply sell your address.

use_cases.example: A store account starts with one tap and a forwarding email, so promo mail never hits your main inbox.
A social app creates your profile from your Apple name without asking you to type it.
A game ties your save file to your Apple account so it restores on a new iPhone.
A news app uses a relay email so it can send newsletters, and you can turn them off at the source.
A dating app signs you up faster and sees only the name you choose to share.
A marketer finds relay emails harder to match across companies, which weakens cross app tracking.

story.android_note: Android apps show a Credential Manager sheet and may offer Sign in with Apple through the web.
story.ios_note: iPhone apps get the native Apple button, with a required relay email option when it is used.

story.what_it_is: Your phone shows a short message when an app has read what you copied.

marketing.name: Paste notification
marketing.pitch: iOS tells you when an app has pasted from another app, so you see who touches your clipboard.

story.for_makers: Makers must now explain why they read your clipboard, since the banner is public. It scared away many sneaky reads. A well timed read after a button tap feels normal, one on launch looks suspicious.

use_cases.example: A chat app reads a copied link only after you press paste, so no banner scares you.
A game that reads copied text on every launch triggers a banner and loses trust.
A shopping app that peeks at copied text on launch would trigger a banner, so careful ones wait until you tap paste.
News apps were shown reading the clipboard on launch when the banner first appeared in 2020.
A security tool lists which apps read your clipboard, so you can spot odd behavior.
A developer uses the paste button instead, which needs no banner and no permission.

story.ios_note: iPhone shows a banner after the paste and also gates it with an Allow Paste prompt.

marketing.pitch: iOS 16 asks before an app reads the clipboard from another app. A system paste button avoids the prompt.

story.for_makers: Makers who want a smooth paste use the system Paste button, because tapping it counts as consent and the popup never shows. Apps that read the clipboard on launch get the popup and look pushy. It pushes honest design.

A shopping app has a Paste link field so you can search by a copied product link.

story.for_makers: Makers and ad firms use it to count people when no ID is allowed, and to spot fraud and bots. It is accurate but breaks easily, and app stores treat the tracking use as a policy violation.

limits.headline: Can match you across apps and sites using your email or phone, scrambled into an ID
limits.user_action: You sign in or give your email or phone to an app or site
can: Turn your email or phone into a scrambled code and share that code with ad partners
Recognize you in other apps and websites that use the same system
Work on both Android and iPhone through ad SDKs and server to server links
cannot: Match you if you never give an email or phone to any partner
Match you when you use Hide My Email; Apple's relay address breaks the link
Use your real email directly; partners share the scrambled version
Work after you opt out where the ID provider offers an opt out
limits.reach_label: Follows you across apps and sites
limits.differs: Hide My Email on iPhone can break matching. Android sign in gives apps your real email.

story.what_it_is: Ad companies turn your email or phone into a shared scrambled ID that follows you across apps and sites.

marketing.name: UID2
marketing.pitch: Pitch: an open ID built from an email or phone that lets advertisers reach people on the open internet with privacy controls.

story.for_you: You type your email to read an article or sign in to a shopping app. Later, ads on other apps and sites may seem to know you. You never see the scrambled ID that links them.
story.for_makers: With device IDs fading, a login is the best key for ads. Publishers sell logged in audiences, and advertisers match their customer lists to them. It only works when people sign in.

use_cases.example: A news site asks you to sign in with an email, then sells ad space to brands that can recognize you by a scrambled copy of it.
A retailer uploads its customer list to an ad network so you see its ads on other apps.
A streaming service lets advertisers reach logged in viewers across phone and TV.
A brand measures whether a TV ad made a known customer buy later in an app.
A game with a login shares a hashed email with an ad partner to find look alike players.
Fraud teams check if one hashed email is tied to hundreds of fake sign ups.

risks: Follows you across apps and sites
story.android_note: Works the same way on Android, with the ad ID as one more signal.
story.ios_note: Works on iPhone too. Sign in with Apple's hidden email stops it.

technical_bounds: Needs a signed-in user
Consent regimes apply
Apple relay emails cannot be matched

abuse: Linking users across apps without disclosure

history.change: ATT pushes advertisers to log-in-based IDs
Mobile SDKs released for Android and iOS

capabilities.name: Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email
capabilities.plain: Apple signs the person in and can give the app a random relay email instead of the real one.
capabilities.meaning: Stops the app from using email as a cross-site key; hash matching in UID2 and RampID fails against relay addresses.

android.note: Credential Manager and Google Sign-In return the real email.

ios.prompt_ui: Share My Email or Hide My Email
ios.revocation: Settings > Apple ID > Sign in with Apple
ios.store_policy: App Review 4.8: offer an equivalent login if you offer other logins (relaxed Jan 2024)
ios.note: Developers must register email domains/senders with Apple to relay mail.

data.metric: Stable per-team user ID and optional relay email

limits.headline: Can sign you in on iPhone and give the app a random relay email instead
limits.user_action: You tap Sign in with Apple and choose Share My Email or Hide My Email
can: Sign you in with your Apple account
Give the app your real email, if you pick Share My Email
Give the app a random relay address, if you pick Hide My Email
Forward the app's emails to you through Apple's relay
cannot: Reveal your real email when you pick Hide My Email
Send email to you unless the developer registered its sending domain with Apple
Work on Android; Google Sign-In and Credential Manager return the real email
limits.differs: iPhone only. Android sign in always returns your real email.

story.what_it_is: Apple signs you in and can give the app a random fake email that forwards to you.

marketing.name: Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email
marketing.pitch: Pitch: sign in quickly and keep your real email private with a random address that forwards to you.

marketing.name: Hide My Email
marketing.pitch: Support page: create unique random email addresses that forward to your inbox, so you do not share your real one.

story.for_you: You tap Sign in with Apple, use Face ID, and pick Hide My Email. The app gets a random address that forwards to you. You can turn it off any time, which stops that app's emails.
story.for_makers: Makers get a fast sign up with less typing and fewer fake accounts. They lose the real email as a way to link people across ads and sites, and they must send mail through Apple's relay.

use_cases.example: You sign up for a store and give it a random address, so a data leak or sale of its list never exposes your real email.
A game offers Sign in with Apple so you start in seconds and keep your email private.
A newsletter site uses the relay so you can cut off emails with one tap in Settings.
A dating app lets you sign up without sharing your main email or phone.
An ad firm cannot match a relay address to the same person's other accounts.
Apple's sign in lowers fake account sign ups because each one needs a real Apple account.

risks: Apps may force an Apple account
story.android_note: Android has no matching feature. Google offers its own Sign in with Google with real emails.
story.ios_note: Built into iOS and Apple accounts. Developers must offer it when they offer other social sign ins.

technical_bounds: Real name only on first sign in
Relay needs sender registration

legit_uses: Account creation without handing out an email
abuse: Marketing with a real email via consent

history.change: Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email
Token revocation required for account deletion (30 June 2022)

capabilities.name: iCloud Private Relay and in-app traffic
capabilities.plain: iCloud Private Relay hides the IP in Safari and some cleartext traffic, but not most app traffic.
capabilities.meaning: Click-side IPs from Safari differ from the app's own IP, hurting probabilistic matching. Apps still see the real IP in their own requests.

android.note: Android has no Private Relay equivalent; VPN or Private DNS only.

ios.note: Covers Safari, DNS queries and unencrypted app HTTP, not HTTPS app traffic.

limits.headline: Can't hide your IP in most iPhone app traffic, only in Safari and some other traffic
limits.user_action: Nothing. You turn iCloud Private Relay on in iPhone settings
can: Hide your real IP in Safari browsing when you have it on
Hide DNS lookups and unencrypted app web traffic
Give you the same coverage on your iPhone, iPad and Mac with iCloud+
cannot: Hide your IP in most app traffic; secure app connections go direct
Work on Android; use a VPN or Private DNS there
Stop the app from seeing your account, device ID or what you type
Cover everything; Apple's own service decides what goes through
limits.differs: Private Relay is an iPhone feature with iCloud+. Android has no equivalent; people use a VPN or Private DNS.

story.what_it_is: Apple hides your network address in Safari, but most app traffic is not covered.

marketing.name: iCloud Private Relay
marketing.pitch: Pitch: when you browse in Safari, your IP address and browsing activity are protected so no one can build a profile of you.

story.for_you: With Private Relay on, websites in Safari see only a rough region instead of your real address. Most apps still see your real network address, so they can still know roughly where you are.
story.for_makers: Makers who count on IP addresses for ads, fraud checks and install matching find Safari clicks harder to link to app opens. Inside their own apps, they still see the real address, so most tools keep working.

use_cases.example: An install tracker wanted to match a Safari ad click to an app open by network address, but the two now show different addresses.
A bank wanted to flag a login from a far city using the network address. Relay hides the real one in Safari, so it relies on other checks.
A streaming site that blocks by country sees a nearby relay address and may allow or block the wrong people.
A web game with regional servers picks a server by region instead of exact location.
A store that sets prices by city sees only a coarse area from Safari.
A news site that counts unique visitors by address sees groups, not single people.

risks: Gives a false sense of full cover
story.android_note: Android has no matching built in Google feature that hides your address for all browsing.
story.ios_note: A paid iCloud+ feature. It covers Safari, unencrypted app traffic and some DNS, not most app traffic.

technical_bounds: Real IP visible to HTTPS app traffic
Safari click and app IP mismatch

history.change: iCloud Private Relay (beta) launched with iCloud+

capabilities.name: Shared Keychain access groups and app groups
capabilities.plain: Apps from one developer team can share secrets and files; other developers cannot join.
capabilities.meaning: Lets one company recognize the same person across its own apps. It cannot see another company's keychain items.

android.api_surface: android:sharedUserId (deprecated API 29), signature permissions, shared content providers
android.note: No direct match. Same signing key apps can share through providers.

ios.api_surface: Keychain access groups, App Groups containers, UserDefaults(suiteName:)
ios.note: Group IDs start with team prefix (keychain) or group. (app groups). Same Apple Developer team only.

limits.headline: Can share saved secrets and files between apps from the same developer on iPhone
limits.user_action: Nothing. The developer sets this up before the app ships
can: Share a login or token between apps from one Apple developer team
Share files and settings through an app group folder
Keep sign in working across a family of apps from the same maker
Share on Android only between apps signed with the same key
cannot: Let apps from other developers join the group
Share across teams; the group name starts with the team prefix
Use sharedUserId on new Android apps; it was deprecated in Android 10
Share on Android with no setup; it needs matching signing keys and a provider
limits.differs: iPhone has built in groups. Android has no direct match and uses same signature sharing.

story.what_it_is: Lets apps from one company on the same phone share passwords, tokens and files.

marketing.name: App Groups
marketing.pitch: Developer guide: let apps from the same team share containers and data on one device.

story.for_you: You sign in once and your other apps from the same company already know you. The upside is smooth use. The downside is that one company can link all of its apps to you without asking.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for single sign on, shared settings and shared downloads between their own apps. Other companies cannot join the group, so it is a safe lane between a developer's own apps.

use_cases.example: You sign in to a mail app and its calendar app from the same company opens already signed in.
A studio shares your save file between its main game and a companion app.
A bank shares a secure login token between its main app and a small widget app.
A music app shares downloaded songs with its car and watch helper apps.
A company shares one login across its work apps so staff sign in once.
A developer uses a shared ID to see that one person uses three of its apps.

story.android_note: Android uses shared user IDs and signing keys for a similar feature, now rarely allowed.
story.ios_note: Needs an Apple entitlement and the same developer team, with no prompt to you.

technical_bounds: Same team only
Requires entitlement

abuse: Cross-app ID inside a brand's family of apps

refs.label: Apple: Sharing access to keychain items

capabilities.name: Keychain and Block Store persistence across reinstall
capabilities.plain: A stored ID that survives uninstall, so a reinstalled app recognizes the person.
capabilities.meaning: iOS Keychain entries remain after the app is deleted. Android needs Block Store or Auto Backup. Used for fraud and abuse limits, and sometimes tracking.

android.api_surface: Auto Backup (6.0), Block Store (Play services 2022), AccountManager
android.note: Cleared on uninstall otherwise; backups may restore app data on a new device.

ios.note: Items stay after uninstall; iCloud Keychain sync is optional. Not shared across different teams.

limits.headline: Can recognize you after a reinstall using an ID that stays behind on your phone
limits.user_action: Nothing. The app saves it quietly the first time you use it
can: Keep an ID in the iPhone Keychain that stays after you delete the app
Keep an ID in Android Block Store or Auto Backup that may come back
Sync the saved item to a new device if iCloud Keychain or Google backup is on
Tell the app you are a returning user
cannot: Share the ID with apps from other developers on iPhone
Survive on Android without backup or Block Store; a normal uninstall clears app data
Stay on a phone after a full wipe or reset
Come back on Android if you turn off backup
limits.differs: iPhone keeps Keychain items after uninstall by default. Android clears them unless backup or Block Store is used.

story.what_it_is: A stored ID that stays after you delete and reinstall the app.

marketing.name: Block Store
marketing.pitch: Developer pitch: keep sign in data across app reinstalls and new devices, with no extra login steps.

story.for_you: You delete an app to start fresh, reinstall it, and it says Welcome back. You will not see the stored ID that told it who you were, and clearing it is not simple.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to stop abuse like repeat free trials, and to keep a person signed in after a reset. Ad and analytics firms also use it to keep a stable ID when the ad ID is blocked.

use_cases.example: A game recognizes a banned cheater who deleted the game and reinstalled, and blocks them again.
A streaming app limits a free trial to once per phone, even after you reinstall.
A store sees your welcome coupon was already used on this phone and does not give it again.
A bank app keeps your device trusted after an update, without a new text code.
A dating app spots someone returning after a ban and stops the new account.
An ad partner joins your pre and post reinstall activity, so attribution stays accurate.

story.android_note: Needs Block Store or Auto Backup. Data can also move to a new phone.
story.ios_note: Keychain items often remain after the app is deleted, unless the developer clears them.

technical_bounds: Apple: only same team; Android: Block Store is per app
Privacy label must declare any identifier collected

history.change: Block Store API released for credentials and IDs

capabilities.name: Mail Privacy Protection and Link Tracking Protection
capabilities.plain: Apple Mail preloads email images through a proxy and Safari and Mail strip known tracking parameters from links.
capabilities.meaning: Open pixels look like opens even when no human saw the email, so email-to-app funnels are noisy. Link Tracking Protection (iOS 17) removes known click IDs from URLs in Mail, Messages and Safari private browsing.

android.note: Gmail and Android do not add equivalent OS-level link stripping.

ios.persistence: Mail Privacy Protection per Mail account setting; Link Tracking Protection default in Mail, Messages, private browsing
ios.note: Link Tracking Protection came with iOS 17; it strips known parameters (for example gclid, fbclid, mc_eid) but not custom ones.

limits.headline: Can't see when you open an email in Apple Mail, and some link tags get stripped
limits.user_action: Nothing. You turn it on in Mail settings and Safari uses it by default
can: Preload email images through Apple's proxy so open tracking is hidden
Strip known tracking tags from links in Safari and Mail on iOS 17 and newer
Hide your IP from the sender when it loads the images
cannot: Strip custom tracking tags, only known ones such as gclid, fbclid and mc_eid
Work in Gmail or other Android mail apps; no matching system feature exists
Stop a sender from knowing you clicked a link they sent
Hide that an email was delivered
limits.differs: This is Apple Mail and Safari only. Android and Gmail have no system wide match.

story.what_it_is: Apple Mail hides when you open an email and strips tracking codes from links.

marketing.name: Mail Privacy Protection
marketing.pitch: Pitch: stops senders from learning if you opened their email and hides your IP address from them.

story.for_you: Marketing emails can no longer tell when you read them or where you are. Links you tap in Mail, Messages and private Safari lose some tracking codes, so what you click is harder to trace.
story.for_makers: Open rates now look high even when no human read the email, so email to app funnels are noisy. Makers lean on clicks, app opens and sign ins instead of the open pixel.

use_cases.example: An advertiser wanted to retarget people who opened its email. Apple Mail now preloads images, so everyone looks like an opener.
A store wanted to send a follow up to people who opened a deal email, and now relies on actual clicks.
A newsletter wanted to find the most engaged readers and now counts link clicks and app opens.
A growth team wanted to see which email led to an app install, and now uses clean links and app events.
A game wanted to email lapsed players if they opened a comeback offer, and now uses push messages.
Phishing senders lose the ability to confirm that a real person opened a scam email.

risks: Marketers may switch to harder tracking
story.android_note: Gmail hides your address by proxying images, but it does not preload every email like Apple Mail does.
story.ios_note: Turned on in Mail settings. Link Tracking Protection came in iOS 17.

technical_bounds: Custom params survive
Universal links pass through unchanged

history.change: Link Tracking Protection in Mail, Messages and Safari Private Browsing

capabilities.name: Probabilistic install matching (IP plus user agent)
capabilities.plain: An MMP guesses which ad click led to an install by matching IP, device model and OS version within a short time window.
capabilities.meaning: Without IDs, the vendor matches the click (IP, UA, language, OS) with the first app open from the same signals, usually within hours. Apple treats this as fingerprinting for ATT-denied users.

android.store_policy: Play does not ban it; used as fallback to referrer
android.api_surface: MMP click redirect + SDK first open
android.note: Used when Install Referrer is not available, e.g. non-Play installs.

ios.store_policy: App Review 5.1.2(i): fingerprinting prohibited for tracking; vendors limit it to non-user-level modeling
ios.note: iCloud Private Relay hides the Safari IP, breaking matches; Apple leaves enforcement to review.

limits.headline: Can guess which ad led to your install by matching your IP, phone model and timing
limits.user_action: You tap an ad, install the app, then open it within a short window
can: Match your ad click to your first open using IP, phone model and system version
Credit the right ad when no exact install code is available
Work for installs outside Google Play on Android and, with gaps, on iPhone
cannot: Match you for sure; it is a guess and can be wrong
Match you on a long delay; it needs a short time window
Match you on iPhone when iCloud Private Relay hides your Safari IP
See anything else about you from this step alone
limits.differs: Android has a reliable referrer for Play installs, so guessing is a backup. On iPhone it is often the main method, though Private Relay breaks it.

story.what_it_is: A guess about which ad led to an install, made by comparing network and device details.
story.for_you: You tap an ad, install the app and the ad firm quietly matches the two by network address and device details. You never see this. It can be wrong, especially on shared Wi-Fi.
story.for_makers: When IDs are blocked, ad firms still need to say which campaign worked. Matching in a short window gives an estimate for budgets. Apple treats it as fingerprinting when the person said no to tracking.

use_cases.example: A game studio checks which of five video ads brought a new player, using the click and first open from the same Wi-Fi.
A retailer measures whether an influencer link caused app installs.
A mobile game pays an ad network per install, and the match decides who gets paid.
Fraud teams spot clicks that claim installs by guessing from the same address at odd hours.
A booking app estimates which search ad led to its first booking in the app.
A marketing team compares the guess to Apple's own aggregate ad reports.

story.android_note: Allowed more freely, though Google Play rules limit ad use.
story.ios_note: Apple warns it counts as fingerprinting for people who tapped Ask App Not to Track.

technical_bounds: Accuracy falls with shared Wi-Fi, VPN, Private Relay
Not allowed on iOS for denied users per Apple

abuse: Joining a click to a device without consent

history.change: ATT: IP+UA matching not allowed for denied users; vendors restrict or rebrand
iCloud Private Relay hides Safari IP from apps' redirectors

capabilities.name: Autoplay audio and video
capabilities.plain: Starts video or sound automatically; muted video is allowed, sound usually needs prior interaction.
capabilities.meaning: A site can start media without a click. Browsers allow silent autoplay but block surprise sound unless the person has engaged with the site, which shapes ad video and background audio.

web.api: <video autoplay muted playsinline>; HTMLMediaElement.play(); allow="autoplay"; navigator.getAutoplayPolicy()

access.persistence: Chrome Media Engagement Index (MEI) score is stored per origin
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Top frame must delegate with allow="autoplay" for cross-origin iframes
steps: Element has muted attribute or origin has activation or high MEI
play() resolves or rejects with NotAllowedError
Handle the rejection and show a play button

limits.headline: Can start muted video on its own, and sound only after you have interacted
limits.user_action: Nothing for muted video. For sound, you tap, click or press a key on the site first
can: Start a silent video without a click
Start sound after you have clicked, tapped or watched on the site
Start a clip after you tap Play
cannot: Play sound on a first visit without any interaction
Keep a sound ad alive in a tab you muted
Override your browser's autoplay setting
Play a video in the background once the page is hidden on most phones
limits.reach_label: Muted video, sound after you interact
limits.differs: Safari and iPhone are strict about sound. Chrome and Edge allow sound for sites you used often. Firefox lets you block it.

story.what_it_is: A page can start video or sound by itself. Muted video is usually fine, sound needs your action first.

marketing.name: Autoplay policy
marketing.pitch: Chrome allows muted autoplay, and lets sound autoplay only after you have interacted with the site.

marketing.name: New video policies for iOS
marketing.pitch: Safari lets muted videos play inline automatically, and requires a tap for videos with sound.

story.for_you: A video on a page may start playing silently as you scroll. Sound normally starts only after you click or tap. Browsers keep this rule to avoid surprise noise.
story.for_makers: Makers use muted autoplay to show previews and grab attention, which raises views and ad time. They ask for a tap before sound. Games need one click before audio. Ads that autoplay can annoy users.

use_cases.example: A streaming home page plays a silent trailer behind the title, so browsing feels alive.
A browser game must wait for your first click or key press before its music and sounds can play.
A social feed starts muted clips as you scroll, and you tap to hear them.
A news site starts a muted video in an article, which many people watch with captions.
A video ad starts muted in the page, and counts a view after a few seconds.
A store plays a muted product video on the page to show the item in use.
A live stream page starts muted and asks you to unmute for sound.
A music site shows a play button, because the browser blocks sound until you tap.

technical_bounds: Muted autoplay is allowed everywhere (iOS also needs playsinline)
Chrome 66: audible autoplay needs user activation on the origin, a high MEI score, or an installed PWA; MEI needs roughly 20 visits and a score of about 0.2 to 0.3 (Chromium source)
MEI counts a play as significant when media plays 7 s or more, is audible, tab active, and video at least 200 by 140 px
Firefox 66 blocks audible autoplay by default (site exceptions allowed); Safari 11 on macOS and iOS 10 block audible autoplay by default
Chrome mutes autoplay in cross-origin iframes unless allow="autoplay" is set

history.change: Block audible autoplay by default on macOS
Autoplay policy: muted allowed; audible needs activation, MEI or PWA
Autoplay policy for media in background tabs unchanged; play() promise rejection documented widely

refs.label: WebKit new video policies for iOS

capabilities.name: Leave-page confirmation (beforeunload)
capabilities.plain: Shows a generic Leave site? dialog, only if the person interacted with the page.
capabilities.meaning: A site can ask the person to confirm closing or leaving, often to protect unsaved work. Browsers hide the site's own text, so it cannot scare people with custom messages.

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Fires on each unload attempt while the listener exists
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Dialog suppressed in cross-origin iframes without activation
steps: Person interacts with the page (sticky activation)
Page registers beforeunload and sets returnValue
On close or navigate, browser shows generic confirmation

limits.headline: Can show a generic Leave site? warning when you close or leave, after you have interacted
limits.user_action: You click, tap or type on the page, then try to close or leave it
can: Show a Leave site? box to protect your unsaved work
Show it when you close the tab or window
Show it when you press back or go to another site
cannot: Show custom text, since browsers hide the site's own message
Show the box if you have not touched the page
Block you for good, since you can still leave
Work on iPhone browsers
limits.differs: Works in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari on computers. iPhone browsers do not show it.

story.what_it_is: A page can show a generic Are you sure you want to leave dialog, only after you used the page.

marketing.name: beforeunload event
marketing.pitch: Lets a page warn before you leave, with a standard message, only if you have interacted with it.

story.for_you: If you try to close a page with unsaved work, a box asks Leave site? You can stay or leave. Pages you never touched cannot show it.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to protect unsaved work in forms, editors and checkouts. Browsers use a fixed message to stop it being used to trap people. Misuse by scam sites is limited by the click rule.

use_cases.example: A web editor like Google Docs warns you if edits are not saved yet when you close the tab.
A checkout page asks if you want to leave with items in your cart and a half filled form.
A browser game asks before you leave a ranked match where leaving counts as a loss.
A web design tool warns about unsynced changes.
A test platform warns a student before they close an exam.
A bank page warns you before you leave a half finished transfer.
A scam page tries to trap you with repeated Leave prompts, but browsers allow it only after you click.

technical_bounds: Needs sticky user activation: no dialog if the page was never clicked or typed in (Chrome 60)
Custom message text is ignored (Chrome 51, Firefox 44, Safari 9.1)
Cannot run async work or block navigation indefinitely: dialog is the only block
A beforeunload listener makes a page ineligible for the back/forward cache in Chrome desktop and Firefox
Not reliable on mobile: tab discard and app switch skip it; use pagehide and visibilitychange

history.change: Dialog requires user interaction with the page

capabilities.name: Compression Streams
capabilities.plain: Compresses or decompresses data in the page with built-in gzip, deflate or deflate-raw.
capabilities.meaning: A site can shrink or expand data without a library. It also lets trackers pack fingerprint payloads before sending them out.

access.persistence: None
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag; available in workers

limits.headline: Can squeeze or unpack data in the page with the browser's built in compression
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a site's script compresses logs, files or data
can: Compress data with gzip or deflate before sending it
Unpack compressed files in the page
Shrink payloads, including tracking data, before they go out
cannot: See your files unless you chose them
Send anything by itself, only change data the page already has
Be turned off from your browser settings
Do heavy work forever, since large tricks can hit memory limits

story.what_it_is: A page can squeeze or unpack data with built in compression, so it sends less over the network.

marketing.name: Compression Streams API
marketing.pitch: Gives pages fast built in gzip and deflate, with no extra code to download.

story.for_you: You never see it. Pages that use it send smaller uploads and open big files faster. It saves time and data.
story.for_makers: Makers drop heavy compression libraries and ship less code. It speeds up uploads, saves and downloads. The same trick can hide the size of data a script sends out, which tracking code can use.

use_cases.example: A browser game compresses save files before uploading them to the cloud, so saves are quick on mobile data.
A web editor compresses documents before sync and saves bandwidth.
A web design tool unpacks large project files in the browser.
A web video app packs frames or clips before an upload.
An analytics script compresses batches of events before sending them in one request.
A web tool lets you drag in a zip or gzip file and view its contents in the page.
A tracking script packs a large fingerprint into a small request that is hard to spot.

technical_bounds: Formats: gzip, deflate, deflate-raw (brotli not in the spec baseline)
Streaming only, no password or zip container; browser does not compress files on disk
DecompressionStream has no output cap; zip bomb risk fills memory
Support: Chrome 80, Safari 16.4, Firefox 113

abuse: Memory exhaustion with a decompression bomb

capabilities.name: Cookie Store API
capabilities.plain: Reads and changes cookies asynchronously and gets change events, including in service workers.
capabilities.meaning: A site can watch and edit its own cookies without parsing document.cookie. It sees only non-HttpOnly cookies for its own origin.

web.api: cookieStore.get(), getAll(), set(), delete(); cookiechange event

access.persistence: Same as the cookie lifetime
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-origin and secure contexts only
steps: cookiechange event fires in other tabs and service workers

limits.headline: Can watch and change the site's own cookies, but not hidden ones or other sites' cookies
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the site's script checks or sets a cookie
can: List and change the site's own cookies that scripts may see
Get a notice when its own cookies change, including in a background script
Keep your sign in in step across tabs
cannot: See other sites' cookies
See protected cookies marked HttpOnly
Work from outside the site's own address
Be sure to stop cookie syncing, which you stop by clearing cookies or blocking trackers

story.what_it_is: A page can read and change cookies the modern way and hear about changes, even in background scripts.

marketing.name: Cookie Store API
marketing.pitch: Offers an async way to read and write cookies and to listen for changes, including in service workers.

story.for_you: You never see it. Sites use it to remember your login and settings. If you clear cookies, the site will see the change.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to manage login, consent choices and tracking IDs without blocking the page. Change events let them react when cookies are added or cleared. It works inside background scripts too.

use_cases.example: A store keeps your cart and login in cookies, and notices if they are cleared to rebuild your session.
An ad script watches for cookie changes and re-creates its ID if you clear it.
An analytics tool reads and writes its visitor ID cookie, and sends a new event when it changes.
A browser game portal stores your sign in and settings in cookies, and syncs across tabs.
A bank page detects when its session cookie is removed and logs out the tab.
A news site stores your cookie consent choices and reads them in the background scripts.
A streaming site shares a login across tabs using cookie change events.

technical_bounds: HTTPS only; cannot read HttpOnly cookies
Cookie size limit 4096 bytes for name plus value; about 180 cookies per domain in Chrome, 50 per domain in Firefox (older), 150 in Safari
Max Expires/Max-Age cap is 400 days in Chrome (Chrome 104)
Third-party contexts follow normal third-party cookie blocking and the Storage Access API
Support per MDN BCD: Chrome and Edge 87, Safari 18.4, Firefox 140

history.change: Cookie Max-Age and Expires capped at 400 days
Cookie Store API ships in Safari
Cookie Store API ships in Firefox

capabilities.name: Cross-origin isolation (SharedArrayBuffer, COOP, COEP)
capabilities.plain: A site can opt into an isolated mode that unlocks SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers and Wasm threads.
capabilities.meaning: Isolation trades openness (no cross-origin popups or unmarked embeds) for power. Sites with it get memory sharing and 5 microsecond timers, which are also better side channel tools.

web.api: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin; Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp or credentialless; self.crossOriginIsolated

access.persistence: Set per document via headers
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Embedded frames need CORP or CORS (require-corp) or credentialless mode
steps: Server sends COOP and COEP headers
SharedArrayBuffer and fine timers become available

limits.headline: Can switch on a locked down mode that unlocks fast shared memory for the page
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the site loads with the right security headers set.
can: Share memory between background threads for heavy apps like games and editors
Run the page's own code with very precise timers
Start multi threaded compiled code inside the page
cannot: Open popups that stay linked to other sites while isolation is on
Load embedded videos, ads or widgets that are not marked to allow it
Turn itself on without the site's own server sending the right headers
See anything in other tabs or other sites
limits.differs: Works in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, including on iPhone and Android.

story.what_it_is: A site can switch on a locked down mode that unlocks very fast, shared memory tricks.

marketing.name: Cross-origin isolation
marketing.pitch: Chrome's web.dev guide says isolation unlocks powerful features like SharedArrayBuffer and high precision timers, in exchange for stricter rules about embeds.

story.for_you: You never see a prompt. A big web app just runs smoother, but some embedded widgets, like a video or ad frame, may refuse to load until their owners add the right labels.
story.for_makers: Makers flip this on to get shared memory and multi threaded compiled code, which game engines and heavy editors need. The cost is that every third party embed on the page must opt in too, which is a real project for ad heavy sites.

use_cases.example: A Unity or Unreal game exported to the browser uses several worker threads at once, which only works when the page is isolated.
A web video editor trims and renders clips using many CPU threads so the preview stays smooth.
Spreadsheets and CAD tools in the browser share one big block of memory between workers to crunch numbers faster.
An in browser coding sandbox runs a whole Node style environment and needs shared memory to do it.
Security teams use isolation to make sure that a page cannot be read by other sites' scripts, a defence against Spectre style attacks.
Ad networks must retag their frames and scripts so a publisher can turn isolation on without breaking ad slots.

technical_bounds: SharedArrayBuffer requires crossOriginIsolated (Chrome 92, Firefox 79, Safari 15.2)
COEP require-corp: every subresource needs CORP or CORS; credentialless mode available in Chrome 96 and Firefox 119
COOP same-origin severs window.opener to cross-origin popups (breaks OAuth popups unless same-origin-allow-popups)
Isolated pages get performance.now at 5 microsecond resolution (Chrome) instead of 100 microseconds
Chrome on Android got SharedArrayBuffer under the same rule in 92

abuse: Fast timer side channels (Spectre style) if isolation fails

capabilities.name: alert, confirm and prompt dialogs
capabilities.plain: Blocks the page with a modal alert, confirm or prompt box.
capabilities.meaning: A site can interrupt the person with a message or a text box. Dialogs freeze the page script, are easy to abuse, and are blocked in cross-origin iframes and background tabs.

access.persistence: One-shot; Chrome adds Prevent this page from creating more dialogs after repeats
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Blocked in cross-origin iframes in Chrome 92 and later; sandboxed frames need allow-modals
steps: Browser shows modal dialog and blocks the page thread
Return value goes back to script

limits.headline: Can freeze the page with a pop up message box until you answer it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page runs a script, or after an action like Delete.
can: Show an alert, a yes or no question or a box asking you to type text
Pause the page until you tap OK or Cancel
Ask Are you sure you want to leave? before you close the tab
cannot: Show the box on tabs you are not looking at in most browsers
Pause other tabs or other apps
Fill your screen with endless boxes; browsers let you block more from that page
See what you type into other sites
limits.reach_label: One page, one box at a time

story.what_it_is: A site can pop up a message box that freezes the page until you click.
story.for_you: You see a grey box that says something like 'Leave site?' or 'Are you sure?' and the page stops until you answer. Scam sites use fake versions to scare you.
story.for_makers: Makers use these for the simplest possible yes or no and for quick debugging. Browsers now limit them, so serious apps build their own dialogs instead.

use_cases.example: An online editor asks 'Discard unsaved changes?' when you try to close the tab.
A checkout page asks 'Are you sure you want to leave? Your cart will be lost.'
A fake 'Your computer is infected, call this number' alert loops on a scam site until you force quit.
A developer drops quick alert boxes into code to see a value while testing.
A simple browser game confirms 'Restart level?' before wiping your progress.
An old internal admin tool asks 'Delete 40 records?' with a plain browser confirm box.

technical_bounds: Cross-origin iframe dialogs are blocked in Chrome 92 (and Safari, Firefox have similar restrictions); same-origin iframes still allowed
Dialogs from background tabs are queued until the tab is foregrounded in Chrome
Chrome shows a Prevent this page from creating more dialogs checkbox on repeated dialogs
Dialog text is plain text, no HTML; Chrome shows the origin in the title
Modal blocks the whole event loop of the tab (and other same-process tabs may freeze)

abuse: Dialog loops that trap the tab

history.change: Cross-origin iframe alert, confirm, prompt blocked
Dialog from background tab queued; tab-modal dialogs introduced earlier

capabilities.name: Trigger file downloads
capabilities.plain: Saves a file to the device; repeated automatic downloads ask permission.
capabilities.meaning: A site can drop files into Downloads (reports, exports, installers). Browsers guard with multi-download prompts and safe browsing checks because a downloaded file is how malware arrives.

access.persistence: Chrome stores Automatic downloads permission per origin after the person allows it
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Sandboxed frames need allow-downloads (Chrome 83); downloads from cross-origin iframes without activation are blocked
steps: Page creates anchor or sends Content-Disposition
Safe Browsing may warn or block

limits.headline: Can save a file to your device, but repeated automatic downloads ask first
limits.user_action: Nothing for the first one. It happens when the page runs a download or you tap a link.
can: Save a file to your Downloads folder when you tap a download link
Make a file on the spot, such as a receipt or a report, and save it
Start one download without asking in most browsers
cannot: Save many files in a row without a second prompt asking you to allow it
Open or run the file for you; you still have to open it
Save the file anywhere except the browser's download location
Skip the browser's warning for risky file types
limits.reach_label: One file, then it asks again
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox ask before several automatic downloads. Safari on iPhone shows a download button for each file.

story.what_it_is: A site can save a file to your device, and the browser asks if it keeps doing it.
story.for_you: You click a button and a file lands in your Downloads folder. If a page tries to download many files by itself, the browser asks whether to allow that.
story.for_makers: Makers build files in the page (a report, an image, an export) and hand them over with one click. It saves server work and lets apps feel like desktop programs.

use_cases.example: You hit Export on a spreadsheet web app and it makes the CSV file right inside your browser.
A design tool saves your finished artwork as a PNG or PDF straight from the page.
Your bank offers a statement as a PDF download for your tax records.
A browser game lets you download your save file so you can move it to another computer.
A malicious site tries to push a file you did not ask for, which is why browsers warn on repeated automatic downloads.
A web video editor renders your clip and downloads the MP4 when it is done.

technical_bounds: download attribute is ignored for cross-origin URLs (Chrome 65, Firefox); filename comes from the response then
Second and later downloads without a click trigger Chrome's Automatic downloads prompt (Firefox shows a similar download panel)
Chrome blocks downloads from sandboxed iframes without allow-downloads (Chrome 83) and insecure (HTTP) downloads on HTTPS pages (Chrome 86 to 88)
Cannot choose the download folder; cannot open the file; dangerous file types get a warning
Blob URLs and data: URIs for large files are limited by memory (Chrome about 2 GB single Blob); stream with FSA or Streams for bigger files

history.change: download attribute ignored for cross-origin URLs
Downloads in sandboxed iframes need allow-downloads
Mixed-content downloads blocked in phases (executables first in Chrome 88)

refs.label: Chrome download restrictions in sandboxed iframes

capabilities.name: Drag and drop
capabilities.plain: Lets people drag items within or into the page, and lets the page start drags.
capabilities.meaning: A site can start a drag with text, links or files, and react when people drop things on it. Data in a drag is readable only on drop, so the page cannot spy on a drag it does not own.

web.api: dragstart, dragover, drop events; DataTransfer; draggable=true

access.persistence: Per drag operation
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Dragging across iframes allowed; dropped data readable only in the drop handler
steps: Person drags an item over the page
dragover must call preventDefault to accept

limits.headline: Can let you drag items on the page, or drop files onto it
limits.user_action: You drag a file, text or picture onto the page, or drag an item inside it.
can: Accept files you drop onto the page, such as photos or documents
Let you rearrange items by dragging, like cards or lists
Start a drag so you can pull text or an image out of the page
cannot: See your files before you drop them
See files you did not drop
Browse your folders on its own
Take over dragging from other apps or windows

story.what_it_is: People can drag things around the page, or drop files onto it.

marketing.name: HTML Drag and Drop API
marketing.pitch: MDN explains that pages can make items draggable and react when you drop files or text on them.

story.for_you: You pick up a card, a file or a photo with your mouse or finger and drop it somewhere else. It feels natural, so you rarely think about it.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to make web apps feel like real software: reordering lists, uploading by dropping a file, building layouts. It also boosts upload completion because dropping is easier than browsing folders.

use_cases.example: You drag a task card from To Do to Done in a project board.
You drop a photo onto a design canvas and it appears where you let go.
You drag pieces on a browser puzzle or card game, like moving a card in solitaire.
You drag a file into a chat window to send it.
You drag songs into a playlist order on a web music player.
You drag a product into a wish list or onto a compare bar.

risks: Dropped files read by the page

technical_bounds: dataTransfer is in protected mode outside drop: types are visible, data is not readable until drop
Cannot start an OS file drag from the page except the Chrome only DownloadURL type trick
Dropped files expose name, size, type, lastModified; no full path
Touch support: iOS Safari 11 (iPad and iPhone); Android Chrome supports long-press drag since Chrome 96 on some devices
Drag image limited to a rendered element or image; size capped by the OS

abuse: Exfil of dropped sensitive files into the wrong site

history.change: Touch drag and drop on iOS 11 and iPadOS

refs.label: MDN HTML Drag and Drop API

capabilities.name: Fenced frames
capabilities.plain: Embeds content that cannot talk to or be read by the page around it.
capabilities.meaning: Used by ad auctions so the embedding page cannot see which ad rendered. It separates the frame's storage and messaging from the parent to block link-back tracking.

access.persistence: While the frame lives
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Needs opt-in headers (Supports-Loading-Mode: fenced-frame)
steps: Browser loads from URN or opaque URL
Frame cannot read parent, parent cannot read frame

limits.headline: Can embed a box of content that the page around it cannot look into
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, usually where an ad or a widget sits.
can: Show an ad or widget inside the page
Keep the embedded content walled off from the host site
Let ad systems pick an ad without sharing your details with the page
cannot: Share what is inside the box with the page around it
Send scrolling or clicks to the host site beyond what the rules allow
Work in Firefox or Safari, including on iPhone
Be used by every site yet; it is still limited and new
limits.reach_label: A sealed box inside the page
limits.differs: Only Chrome based browsers support it today. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: A box inside a page that is sealed off, so neither side can read the other.

marketing.name: Fenced Frame
marketing.pitch: Chrome's Privacy Sandbox docs describe it as a frame that can show content without sharing information with the embedding page.

story.for_you: You see an ad or embed as normal. What you cannot see is that the page around it is blocked from learning which ad it is, which was meant to stop sites linking your browsing across pages.
story.for_makers: It lets ad tech pick an ad using your interests without handing your identity to the publisher. Advertisers still get counts of views and clicks through special reports, so measurement stays alive.

use_cases.example: An interest based ad is chosen in your browser and shown in a sealed frame, so the news site cannot see which ad you were shown.
An ad network counts that an ad was shown, using a limited summary report instead of a per person log.
A payment or login widget is shown in a frame that the host page cannot peek inside.
A publisher runs an ad slot on an article page without ever learning your ad profile.
A retailer retargets you with a product you viewed, without the news site you are reading ever seeing it.
A browser game shows rewarded video ads in a sealed frame so the ad cannot read the game page.

technical_bounds: No postMessage or storage sharing with the embedder; no access to the DOM from the parent
Fixed size rules for opaque URLs (no custom size) when used with auctions
Privacy Sandbox APIs were deprecated by Google in 2025; the feature remains in Chrome but ecosystem use is shrinking (verify current status)
Supported only in Chromium

abuse: Opaque ads that hide content from site owners

history.change: Fenced frames ship with Privacy Sandbox
Google announces sunset of Privacy Sandbox ad APIs

capabilities.name: Focus and window raise
capabilities.plain: Can move focus between elements; cannot pull the window to the front or steal focus from other apps.
capabilities.meaning: A page can focus its own elements, but browsers stop it from grabbing focus from the address bar, another tab or another app, which blocks keystroke capture and pop-over scams.

access.persistence: None
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframes cannot call focus() on parent or take focus without activation (Chrome 64)
steps: Browser moves focus only inside the page or when the window is already active

limits.headline: Can move the cursor between boxes on its page, but can't pull its window forward
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you use the page, or when it finishes loading.
can: Move the typing cursor to a form box on its own page
Bring its own tab back into focus after you click on it
Highlight a button or field after you finish a step
cannot: Pull its browser window above your other apps
Steal typing from another app or another site
Jump to the front when you are in a different tab
Force a tab to open in front of the one you are in

story.what_it_is: A page can move the typing cursor between its own fields but cannot yank your whole window forward.
story.for_you: A search box can be ready to type the moment a page opens. A site cannot pull itself in front of the game or document you are using in another app.
story.for_makers: Makers use autofocus to save you a click on login and search forms. Browsers block pushing the window to the front to prevent pop under annoyances.

use_cases.example: A store's search bar is ready for typing the moment the page loads.
A browser game grabs keyboard focus on load so arrow keys work without a click.
A chat app puts the cursor in the message box after you open a conversation.
