capabilities.name: Keyboard Lock
capabilities.plain: Captures keys like Escape and Alt+Tab while in fullscreen.
capabilities.meaning: Lets games and remote desktops receive keys the browser normally keeps, so a site can trap Escape or Ctrl+W. Works only in fullscreen; a long-press of Escape always exits.

access.prompt_ui: No prompt; works only while the page is in fullscreen.
access.persistence: While in fullscreen
access.iframe: Frames inherit fullscreen
steps: Locked keys sent to the page

limits.headline: Can capture keys like Escape and Alt+Tab while the page is full screen
limits.user_action: You tap a full screen button in a game or remote desktop
can: Take over keys the browser normally keeps, such as Escape or Alt+Tab
Pass those keys to a game or remote desktop session
Do this only while the page is in full screen
cannot: Trap you for good; holding Escape for about 2 seconds always lets you out
Capture keys when the page is not full screen
Work in Firefox or Safari
Capture the operating system's own protected shortcuts like Ctrl+Alt+Delete
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge support it on desktop. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: Lets a page grab keys like Escape and Alt+Tab when full screen.

marketing.name: Keyboard Lock
marketing.pitch: Describes a way for web apps in full screen to capture keys the browser normally keeps, helpful for games and remote desktops.

story.for_you: You go full screen in a game or remote desktop and keys like Escape go to the game instead of closing it. A message usually says 'Hold Escape to exit full screen'. You feel the page has taken over your keyboard.
story.for_makers: Cloud games and remote work tools need every key to reach the remote computer. Without it, a press of Escape or Alt+Tab would break the stream. Makers also like how it keeps players inside the app.

use_cases.example: A cloud gaming stream sends Escape, Alt and Windows keys to the remote PC, so an in game menu opens instead of exiting full screen.
A remote desktop in the browser forwards Alt+Tab and Ctrl+W to the remote Windows machine.
A browser strategy or shooter game uses Escape for its pause menu while full screen.
An online exam tool locks a student in full screen so keys cannot switch tabs.
A web video editing or 3D tool receives all shortcuts while in full screen.
A bad page could try to trap you in full screen, which is why the browser shows a hold to exit message.

risks: Can trap you in full screen

technical_bounds: Fullscreen only
Cannot capture Ctrl+Alt+Del or OS shortcuts
Chromium only

abuse: Trapping people in a fullscreen scam page

capabilities.name: Keyboard Map (layout leak)
capabilities.plain: Reveals the physical-to-printed key mapping, i.e. the keyboard layout.
capabilities.meaning: Shows which keyboard layout the person uses (QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak, language), a strong locale and fingerprint signal. No prompt.

access.prompt_ui: No prompt; Chromium exposes it to secure contexts.
access.persistence: n/a
access.iframe: Needs allow="keyboard-map"
steps: Read KeyboardLayoutMap of key codes to characters

limits.headline: Can tell your keyboard layout, which hints at your country and language
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page or app loads
can: Check which character each physical key produces
Guess your language or region from that layout
Add to a profile of your device to help recognise you
cannot: See what you type
Work in Firefox or Safari
Show a permission pop up; there is none
Work outside secure (https) pages
limits.differs: Only Chrome and Edge on desktop support it. Firefox, Safari and most phones do not.

story.what_it_is: Reveals which physical key makes which letter, so the page learns your keyboard layout.
story.for_you: You see nothing. The page quietly learns whether your keyboard is QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak or another layout. No prompt appears. It may be used to guess your country.
story.for_makers: Makers of games and editors use it for correct key labels. Fraud and tracking systems also use it as a free hint to your language, and in a fingerprint it adds a few bits of uniqueness.

use_cases.example: A browser game rebinds its movement keys to fit a Dvorak or AZERTY keyboard so players are not stuck with wrong keys.
A music web app maps piano keys to the correct physical row on any layout.
An ad network adds the layout to a profile and guesses a user's language when other signals are missing.
A fingerprinting script mixes layout, fonts and screen size to spot returning visitors.
A fraud engine flags an order that claims to be in Germany but types on a Russian layout.
A coding web app shows the correct shortcut key names for each layout.

technical_bounds: Chromium only
No key press data

legit_uses: Showing correct key hints in games

capabilities.name: Local Font Access
capabilities.plain: Asks to list every font installed on the device.
capabilities.meaning: Reveals the full list of installed fonts and raw font files, which identifies the device and installed software. Gated by prompt because font lists were a long-standing fingerprint.

access.prompt_ui: Chrome prompt: See fonts on your device, Allow or Block; needs a gesture.
access.persistence: Persistent per origin
access.iframe: Needs allow="local-fonts" in iframes
steps: Array of FontData with family, fullName, postscriptName, style, blob()

limits.headline: Can list the fonts installed on your computer, after you allow it
limits.user_action: You tap a font picker button and choose Allow when Chrome asks
can: See the names of all installed fonts
Open the font files so the page can use them
Show your own fonts in a design or editing tool
cannot: Do this without a tap and your Allow
See the list in Firefox or Safari
Keep access after you pick Block
limits.reach_label: Once you allow it for that site
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge on desktop only. Firefox, Safari and phones do not support it.

story.what_it_is: A site asks to list the fonts installed on your computer.

marketing.name: Local Font Access API
marketing.pitch: Chrome pitches it as a way for design and editing web apps to use fonts installed on the computer, as desktop apps do.

story.for_you: A prompt asks whether the site can see fonts on your device. If you allow, it can list them and use them in your design. If you say no, you only get the standard web fonts.
story.for_makers: Design and publishing tools need access to a person's own fonts, especially brand fonts. The same list of fonts is a strong fingerprint, which is why browsers ask first.

use_cases.example: A web design tool lets a designer pick a licensed brand font that is installed on their laptop.
A web document editor shows a user's own fonts so a file looks the same as on the desktop.
A photo or video web editor loads installed fonts so titles match a project made earlier on the desktop.
A level editor or branded card game maker uses local fonts for custom text in a creation tool.
A fingerprinting script reads the list of fonts to build a nearly unique ID for the device.
A fraud tool compares fonts with the claimed device model, since a Mac should not show Windows fonts.

technical_bounds: Chromium desktop only
Needs gesture and prompt

linkedin.how: LinkedIn probes fonts by metric measurement, not through this permission

capabilities.name: Paste event (read what the person pastes)
capabilities.plain: Gives the page the clipboard contents, but only when the person presses paste inside the page.
capabilities.meaning: A paste is consent for that one read: the site gets text, HTML or files the person chose to paste. It cannot peek at the clipboard at other times, which blocks silent snooping.

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Per paste action
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Fires in the focused frame only
steps: Person presses Ctrl or Cmd+V (or the context menu Paste)
Page reads clipboardData: text, html, files

limits.headline: Can get what you paste, but only when you press paste on its page
limits.user_action: You press Ctrl+V, Cmd+V, or use Paste from the menu on the page
can: Receive text, HTML or files that you paste
Fill in a form field or an editor with it
Work without any pop up
cannot: See your clipboard when you did not paste
See what you pasted on other pages or apps
Get more than the one paste you did
limits.reach_label: One paste, when you press it

story.what_it_is: The page gets what you paste, but only when you press paste on it.

marketing.name: Clipboard events
marketing.pitch: Describes the paste event that gives pages the clipboard content when the person pastes into them.

story.for_you: You paste into a page with Ctrl+V or a right click and the content appears. Pasting counts as your yes for that one time. The page cannot peek at your clipboard at other times.
story.for_makers: Makers let people paste screenshots, tables and links into editors, chats and forms. They can also clean up pasted content or paste formatted text and images safely.

use_cases.example: A chat app lets you paste a screenshot from your clipboard right into the message box.
A document editor pastes a copied web table and keeps its columns.
A design tool turns a pasted image or SVG into a layer on the canvas.
A level editor or modding site lets you paste a map code into a box and loads it.
A site may block pasting into password or code fields, which annoys people with password managers.
A form tool records whether you pasted an email or typed it, as one more signal about bots.

technical_bounds: Only fires on a user paste in the focused document; scripts cannot trigger it with dispatchEvent for real data
Types readable: text/plain, text/html, text/uri-list and files (images, documents)
Pasted HTML is the browser sanitized form, not raw source from the source app
No permission prompt (the keystroke is the consent)
Pasted files expose name, size, type, lastModified; no path

legit_uses: Paste images into chat or docs
abuse: Capturing a sensitive clipboard after social engineering to press paste

history.change: paste event with clipboardData files for images

capabilities.name: Pointer events (mouse, pen, touch detail)
capabilities.plain: Reports pointer position and, for pens and touch, pressure, tilt and contact size.
capabilities.meaning: Mouse paths, speed and hesitation are strong behavioral signals (bot detection, attention tracking). Pen and touch fields add pressure and tilt that can tell devices apart.

web.api: pointerdown/move/up; PointerEvent.pressure, tiltX, tiltY, width, height, pointerType; getCoalescedEvents(); pointerrawupdate

access.persistence: While the pointer is over the page
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Events go to the frame under the pointer; no cross-origin leak across frames
steps: Person moves the pointer or touches
pointermove events fire (usually once per frame, or at the device rate with getCoalescedEvents)

limits.headline: Can see where your mouse, finger or pen is and how it moves on the page
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens while you move or tap over the page
can: Follow the path and speed of your mouse, finger or pen
Measure pen pressure, tilt and finger contact size where the device allows it
Tell humans from bots by how you move
Learn where you hesitate or hover
cannot: See where you point on other pages or in other apps
See movement when the page is in the background
Show a permission pop up; there is none
limits.reach_label: Every move while the page is open

story.what_it_is: The page sees where your mouse, pen or finger is, how fast it moves, and how hard you press.

marketing.name: Pointer events
marketing.pitch: Describes one set of events for mouse, pen and touch, with extras like pressure and tilt for pens.

story.for_you: You move, click, draw or swipe and the page responds smoothly. You may not notice it also sees the path your pointer takes and how long you pause. A pen can add pressure and tilt, so lines look natural.
story.for_makers: Mice and pens drive games and creative tools. Makers also study movement patterns to detect bots, find confusing parts of a page and tune ads and layouts.

use_cases.example: A browser game reads mouse position and clicks many times a second for aiming and dragging.
A web drawing tool uses pen pressure and tilt to vary line thickness.
A whiteboard app shows teammates' live cursors by sending pointer positions to others.
A heatmap tool records where visitors move and click to show the busy parts of a page.
A bot detector checks if the mouse path is a perfect straight line, a sign of a script.
An ad network measures hover time over an ad as a sign of attention.
A bank adds mouse habits to its risk score for a login.

technical_bounds: Sees pointer only inside its own viewport (and over its iframes' areas as the iframe's events)
pressure is 0 to 1 (0.5 for devices without pressure while a button is down); tiltX and tiltY are -90 to 90 degrees; twist 0 to 359
Coalesced events can expose input at 120 Hz or more (Chrome 58 and later, Firefox 59, Safari 18.2 per BCD)
pointerType is mouse, pen or touch; width and height reveal finger contact size (CSS px)
No pointer data while the pointer is outside the viewport, except with setPointerCapture or Pointer Lock

history.change: Pointer Events ship in Chrome stable

capabilities.name: Pointer Lock
capabilities.plain: Hides and captures the mouse for games and 3D views.
capabilities.meaning: Gives raw relative mouse movement with unlimited range while the cursor is hidden. With unadjustedMovement the site gets unaccelerated input, a small hardware hint.

access.prompt_ui: Browser shows an on-screen notice and Esc to exit; some platforms prompt on re-lock. Needs a gesture.
access.persistence: Until Esc or unlock
access.iframe: Frame needs allow-pointer-lock in sandbox

data.update: per mouse event (about 125 Hz or higher)

limits.headline: Can hide your mouse pointer and capture its movement for games or 3D views
limits.user_action: You click inside a game or 3D view
can: Hide the pointer and track raw mouse movement
Let you turn a camera or view without hitting the screen edge
Use unaccelerated mouse input if the site asks for it
cannot: Start without a click, tap or key press
Trap you; Esc always gets you out
Keep control after you switch tabs or apps
Work in Safari on iPhone
limits.differs: Chrome, Firefox, Safari on Mac and Android browsers support it. Safari on iPhone does not.

story.what_it_is: A page hides your mouse pointer and reads your raw movement, like in a shooter game.

marketing.name: Pointer Lock API
marketing.pitch: Describes a way for apps to capture the mouse and read how far it moves, used for games, 3D views and maps.

story.for_you: You click on a game and your mouse pointer disappears. You can turn endlessly with no screen edge stopping you. The browser shows a small note and Escape gives the pointer back.
story.for_makers: First person games, 3D viewers and cloud gaming need unlimited relative mouse movement. Makers can offer console quality aim on the web without installing anything.

use_cases.example: A browser shooter hides the pointer and uses raw mouse movement so you can spin the camera freely.
A cloud gaming service passes your raw mouse movement to the remote PC so aim feels right.
A 3D modeling web app locks the pointer while you orbit around an object.
A 3D globe or map site lets you drag without leaving the screen edge.
A remote desktop in the browser shows the host's pointer rather than yours.
Raw mouse deltas let a game study aim patterns, which also reveals cheaters.

technical_bounds: Needs a gesture
Escape always exits

abuse: Locking cursor to a scam page

capabilities.name: Text selection and caret
capabilities.plain: Lets the page see what is selected inside itself and move the cursor; nothing outside the page.
capabilities.meaning: A site knows which of its own words the person highlights, which reveals interest and reading focus. It cannot see a selection in another tab or app.

access.persistence: Live while the page has focus
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Frames see only their own selection; selection in a cross-origin iframe is hidden from the parent
steps: Page reads the Selection and Range

limits.headline: Can see which of its own words you highlight and move your text cursor
limits.user_action: You highlight text or click in a box on the page
can: See the text you select on the page
Move the cursor or change the selection on its own page
Guess what you are interested in from what you highlight
cannot: See selections in other tabs or apps
See what you select when the page is in the background
Show a permission pop up; there is none
limits.reach_label: Only text on its own page

story.what_it_is: The page sees which of its own words you highlight and where your text cursor is.
story.for_you: You highlight text to copy, look up or share. A small menu may pop up near it. You did not know the page could tell which words you picked. It cannot see selections in other tabs or apps.
story.for_makers: Makers use selection to show a share, quote or highlight menu. Reading apps remember highlights and analytics tools learn what people find interesting.

use_cases.example: A long read site shows a 'share this quote' button when a reader highlights a sentence.
An e-reader or course page saves a student's highlights and notes for later.
A document editor uses selection to show a bold or link toolbar.
A word game or learning site checks which word a player picked from a passage.
A publisher counts which lines get highlighted most to see what resonates.
A dictionary or search widget can show an ad or lookup for the exact words you picked.

technical_bounds: Sees selection inside its own document (and same-origin frames) only
Cannot read the selection from the address bar, other tabs, other apps or browser UI
Password fields: selected text of a password input is not exposed by getSelection().toString() but is readable via the field's value to the page owner
selectionchange has no rate limit; it can fire many times per second while dragging
Firefox returns the selection inside inputs only through selectionStart and selectionEnd

capabilities.name: Touch events and touch point count
capabilities.plain: Reports finger positions and the number of touch points the device supports.
capabilities.meaning: navigator.maxTouchPoints separates phones, tablets and touch laptops from plain desktops, a common fingerprint input. Touch radius and force add small device level detail.

web.api: touchstart/move/end; Touch.radiusX, radiusY, force; navigator.maxTouchPoints; 'ontouchstart' in window

access.persistence: While touching
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Events go to the touched frame
steps: Page reads clientX, clientY, radiusX and force

limits.headline: Can see your finger touches and how many touch points your device supports
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you touch the screen, and the touch count is checked on load
can: See where and when your fingers touch the page
Tell a phone, tablet or touch laptop apart from a plain desktop
Learn small details like touch size where supported
cannot: See touches on other pages or apps
See touches while the page is in the background
Work in desktop Safari, which does not have touch events
limits.differs: Chrome, Firefox and Safari on iPhone support them. Safari on Mac does not.

story.what_it_is: The page sees finger touches and how many touch points your device supports.

marketing.name: Touch events
marketing.pitch: Describes events for touch screens that tell pages when and where fingers touch, move and lift.

story.for_you: You tap, swipe and pinch and the page responds. You do not see that the site also learned how many fingers your device can track. That number helps it tell a phone from a laptop.
story.for_makers: Touch drives mobile games, maps and drawing. The touch point count also helps sites guess device type and block fake browsers, so it shows up in fingerprints.

use_cases.example: A mobile browser game turns finger drags into movement and taps into actions, with several fingers at once.
A cloud gaming site draws on screen controller buttons for touch players.
A web map lets you pinch to zoom and two finger rotate.
A drawing app supports multitouch gestures for zoom and undo.
A site checks touch points to split phone, tablet and desktop traffic.
A fraud check flags a browser that claims to be a phone but reports zero touch points.

technical_bounds: maxTouchPoints is 0 on no touch hardware, commonly 5 on phones, 10 on tablets and laptops (up to 20 on some)
TouchEvent constructors exist only on touch capable devices in Chromium; Safari desktop has no TouchEvent
force is 0 to 1 where hardware supports it; radius may be 0 on devices that do not report contact area
touchstart and touchmove listeners on window default to passive in Chrome 56 and Safari 11.1 (cannot cancel scroll)
Cannot read touches outside the page or on the browser UI

history.change: Document level touch listeners passive by default

capabilities.name: Virtual Keyboard API
capabilities.plain: Lets a page control whether the on-screen keyboard resizes the page or overlays it, and show or hide it.
capabilities.meaning: A web app can take over keyboard layout handling and learn the keyboard rectangle. Keyboard height hints at device type and which keyboard (emoji, numeric) is open.

web.api: navigator.virtualKeyboard.overlaysContent; show(); hide(); boundingRect; geometrychange; env(keyboard-inset-height); virtualkeyboardpolicy

access.persistence: While the page runs
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Main frame only; cross-origin iframes cannot control it

limits.headline: Can control how the on screen keyboard moves the page, and show or hide it
limits.user_action: You tap into a text box on a phone or tablet
can: Choose whether the keyboard pushes the page up or covers it
Learn the size and place of the keyboard
Show or hide the on screen keyboard from a tap
cannot: See what you type on the on screen keyboard
Show the keyboard without a tap on the page
Work in Firefox or Safari
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet support it. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: A web app can control whether your on screen keyboard pushes the page up or covers it.

marketing.name: VirtualKeyboard API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes it as a way for web apps to control layout around the on screen keyboard and show or hide it.

story.for_you: You tap a text box and the keyboard slides up. The page may shrink neatly so your message box stays visible, or the keyboard may overlay a game controller. You may not realize the page can also learn how tall the keyboard is.
story.for_makers: Chat, game and editing apps want to keep the box you are typing in on screen. Makers use the keyboard size to place buttons well. The height also hints at the device and keyboard type.

use_cases.example: A chat web app keeps the message box and send button above the keyboard on a phone.
A browser game with touch buttons keeps them in view when the keyboard opens for a chat message.
A mobile document editor keeps the toolbar just above the keyboard.
A checkout page scrolls the field you are typing in so the pay button stays reachable.
A site notes keyboard height as a clue to device model and OS keyboard settings.
A web app lets people using an on screen keyboard with larger text keep fields visible.

technical_bounds: Chromium on Android and ChromeOS only (Chrome 94); no Firefox or Safari
show() and hide() need a focused editable element and (for show) a recent user action
CSS env() variables keyboard-inset-top, -left, -bottom, -right, -width, -height
Cannot read keystrokes or which keyboard app is installed; only the rectangle

capabilities.name: Languages (Accept-Language and navigator.languages)
capabilities.plain: Ordered list of the person's preferred languages, sent on every request.
capabilities.meaning: Shows native language, second languages and country (en-US vs en-GB, es-419). A multilingual list narrows identity sharply: 5.9 bits in 2016. Sites localize with it; trackers fingerprint it.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can see the languages you prefer, in order, with every page request
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser sends it every time a page loads
can: See your first language and backups, such as en-US then es
Show the page in your language
Guess your country from the language variant, such as en-GB or es-419
Add to a profile that helps recognise your browser
cannot: Know your exact location from it
See languages you have not set in your browser
Be turned off on its own; you change it in browser settings

story.what_it_is: Every request tells the site your preferred languages, in order.

marketing.name: Accept-Language
marketing.pitch: Describes the header where browsers list the languages a person prefers so servers can reply in the right one.

story.for_you: You open a site and it appears in your language, or offers a banner to switch. You never see the list of languages your browser sent. If you speak several, that list may be the most telling part.
story.for_makers: Sites use it to pick the language and currency. Ad, fraud and tracking systems also use the exact list as a clue about who you are, since few people share the same mix of languages.

use_cases.example: A game site shows the lobby and rules in your language and puts you in a regional server list.
A cloud gaming site picks the store language and subtitles without asking.
A store shows prices and sizes in your region's format.
A streaming site picks audio and subtitle defaults from your language list.
An ad network targets by language and region, using the list as a profile clue.
A fraud check compares languages with the IP country, since a mismatch may mean a stolen account.
A fingerprinting script mixes the language list with other clues to spot a repeat visitor.

technical_bounds: Browser UI language is not always system language
Single-language lists carry few bits

linkedin.how: Collected as language. Read by the LinkedIn APFC fingerprint script (alleged by BrowserGate, partly confirmed by BleepingComputer).

refs.label: AmIUnique: Beauty and the Beast, Laperdrix et al. 2016 (attribute entropy)

capabilities.name: Accessibility settings inferred
capabilities.plain: Combining contrast, motion, forced colors, zoom and font size to guess a disability.
capabilities.meaning: No single API says disabled, but together prefers-contrast, forced-colors, reduced-motion, large fonts and zoom flag vision, vestibular or motor needs. Under GDPR or similar this may be special-category data.

web.api: Combination of CSS media queries, zoom and font size

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: signals combined
fields.range: forced-colors, prefers-contrast, prefers-reduced-motion, inverted-colors, zoom, font size

limits.headline: Can guess you may use accessibility settings by combining several browser signals
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens quietly while the page loads and you use it
can: Check settings such as high contrast, reduced motion, forced colors, zoom and large text
Guess you may have low vision or need less motion when several signals line up
Change the page design to fit those settings
cannot: Learn for sure that you have a disability
See your medical details or assistive tech by name
Rely on one signal alone; it takes several together

story.what_it_is: Sites can guess a disability from your zoom, contrast, motion and font settings.

marketing.name: prefers-reduced-motion
marketing.pitch: Google teaches pages to honor the person's reduced motion setting so animations can be turned down.

story.for_you: You never see anything. If you use high contrast, large text, big zoom or reduced motion, a site can notice. These settings help you read, but together they can hint at a health or vision condition.
story.for_makers: Makers use these settings to adapt the page for the person, which is the good use. Trackers and ad systems can use the same signals as a clue about health or age, which is sensitive and a privacy risk.

use_cases.example: A site switches to a calmer layout without animation when it sees reduced motion is on.
A browser game turns off screen shake and flashing when it sees reduced motion, and uses stronger contrast colors.
A video site turns on captions and larger controls when contrast and zoom settings suggest low vision.
An ad profile quietly adds 'may have low vision' as a hidden clue to target products, which is a privacy concern.
A fingerprint script uses font size, zoom and contrast as part of a unique ID.
A fraud tool treats odd combinations as a sign of automation or a spoofed browser.

technical_bounds: Only probabilistic; screen reader use is not directly detectable

linkedin.how: BrowserGate alleges extension scan infers disability and neurodivergence; separate from media queries.

capabilities.name: Do Not Track
capabilities.plain: Header and property saying the person asked not to be tracked; mostly ignored.
capabilities.meaning: Reveals a privacy preference (about 1 in 4 desktop Chrome and Firefox users enabled it at its peak) and ironically adds a fingerprint bit. Safari removed it in 12.1; Firefox is removing the setting.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can see whether you turned on Do Not Track, which most sites ignore
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser sends it with each page request if the setting is on
can: Check if you asked not to be tracked
Use the setting as one more clue to recognise your browser
cannot: Make sites stop tracking you; most do not honor it
See the setting in Safari, which removed it
Know why you turned it on
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox still send it if you turn it on. Safari removed it.

story.what_it_is: A setting that tells sites you do not want to be tracked, which most ignore.

marketing.name: Do Not Track
marketing.pitch: Mozilla describes a browser setting that asks sites not to track you, and notes that sites choose whether to respond.

story.for_you: If you turn it on, every site gets a small note saying 'please do not track me'. You see no change. Most sites ignore it, and having it on can make your browser stand out.
story.for_makers: Few makers honor it, because there is no law that requires it. Some analytics tools skip counting those visits. It is also a fingerprint bit, since only some people turn it on.

use_cases.example: A privacy minded analytics tool skips counting visits that carry the request.
An ad network reads the flag and keeps tracking, since no rule forces them to stop.
A news site shows a 'we do not respond to this' note in its privacy policy.
A game site that tracks play time for ads ignores the request, because it is not required to follow it.
A fingerprinting script adds the flag as one more clue to tell visitors apart.
A store records the preference but still uses cookies for the cart.

technical_bounds: No legal force; replaced by GPC

linkedin.how: Do Not Track read but excluded from hash. Read by the LinkedIn APFC fingerprint script (alleged by BrowserGate, partly confirmed by BleepingComputer).

refs.label: AmIUnique: Beauty and the Beast, Laperdrix et al. 2016 (attribute entropy)

capabilities.name: Global Privacy Control
capabilities.plain: Browser signal that the person opts out of sale or sharing of data.
capabilities.meaning: Legally binding opt-out in California, Colorado, Connecticut and more, so sites must honor it. Also tells the site this user runs privacy-focused settings or a browser like Firefox, DuckDuckGo or Brave.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

chrome.note: Not shipped; extensions add the header

firefox.note: Opt-in setting; default in Private Browsing optional

limits.headline: Can see that you asked sites not to sell or share your data
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser sends it with each page request if the setting is on
can: Check the Global Privacy Control signal
Treat it as your opt out of sale or sharing, where the law requires it, such as in California
Learn that you may use a privacy focused browser or setting
cannot: Make a site honor it outside places where the law requires it
See your name or account from this signal

capabilities.meaning: Shows how fast the device turns. Gyroscope noise has been used to eavesdrop on nearby speech (Gyrophone, 2014) and to fingerprint devices, which is why browsers cap the rate.

access.prompt_ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.

steps: 'reading' events fire; 'error' event on NotAllowedError or NotReadableError

Measure turning while the page is closed

story.what_it_is: The page reads how fast your device is turning.

marketing.name: Generic Sensor API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes a common way for web pages to read motion and environment sensors such as accelerometer and gyroscope.

story.for_you: You twist your phone and a game camera turns, or a 360 photo spins. On many phones there is no big prompt. The sensor can also pick up tiny sounds from nearby speech.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for smooth camera control in 3D and AR. Trackers can use sensor quirks to recognize a phone, and research showed it can eavesdrop on speech nearby.

use_cases.example: A browser first person game or 3D viewer turns the camera as you turn your phone.
A web AR try on page uses turning speed to keep models fixed in place.
A 360 degree video pans smoothly as you twist your phone.
A web map turns as you turn, with smooth compass behavior.
Researchers showed a page could pick up speech through gyroscope vibration, an eavesdropping risk.
A fingerprinting script uses tiny gyro errors to recognize one phone among millions.

technical_bounds: 60 Hz cap mitigates the audio side channel
No readings while hidden

history.change: Gyrophone shows speech recovery from gyroscope sampled near 200 Hz

story.for_you: A compass or a map turns to match where you face. You may not see a prompt. Nearby metal and electronics change what the sensor reads.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for compass features and AR. Indoor magnetic patterns can help place a person in a building, and they are also a rough fingerprint of where a device has been.

A site checks for steady human hand motion to catch emulators.

Needs focus and secure context

capabilities.name: Permissions API
capabilities.plain: Lets a page ask what each permission is currently set to without prompting.
capabilities.meaning: navigator.permissions.query() returns granted, denied or prompt for most permissions. It reveals which permissions you have granted or blocked, and a change event lets pages react live.

access.prompt_ui: No prompt; read only. States: granted, denied, prompt. A permissions policy block reports denied.
access.persistence: n/a
access.iframe: Works in iframes; reflects policy

limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page checks a setting

Update the page if you change a setting
Learn which sensors you have allowed on that site

Turn a feature on without your yes

story.what_it_is: Lets a page check whether you already allowed, blocked or never answered a permission, without asking.

marketing.name: Permissions API
marketing.pitch: Docs describe it as a way for pages to check permission status before asking.

story.for_you: You never see it. The page just looks at your earlier answers and decides whether to show a pop-up or a helpful button. It can also see when you change your answer later.
story.for_makers: Asking for a permission at the wrong time annoys people and gets denied for good. The API lets sites ask only when it makes sense, and show a help message when the answer is blocked. It also reveals your settings, which can be used in a fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A video call page checks if the camera is already allowed and skips straight to the call, or shows a how-to-unblock note.
A maps site only shows the Use my location button if location is not blocked.
A browser game asks for microphone access only if it has not been blocked, and shows tips otherwise.
A news site waits to ask about notifications until it knows you have not blocked them.
A fraud tool reads the pattern of allowed and blocked permissions as part of a device profile.
A web app shows a status panel that lists which features are allowed.
A store locator checks location permission before showing a nearby stores prompt.

technical_bounds: Names vary per browser
Permissions.revoke() was removed
Firefox lacks several names such as clipboard-read

capabilities.plain: HTTP header and iframe allow attribute that decide which features a page or frame may use.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a site disable features for itself and its iframes. MDN lists 51 directives; each can be self, a list of origins, or none. A feature blocked here never reaches the user prompt.

access.iframe: Controls iframe delegation

Stop embedded ads or widgets from using sensors
Set 51 or so rules, each for self, listed sites, or none

Skip your pop up for a feature

story.what_it_is: A site rule that says which features the page and its embedded frames are allowed to use.

marketing.name: Permissions Policy
marketing.pitch: Docs explain it as a header that lets sites turn browser features on or off for themselves and embeds.

marketing.name: Permissions Policy
marketing.pitch: Chrome documents how to control feature access for your page and third party frames.

story.for_you: You never see it. Its job is to protect you: a site can promise that an embedded ad or video cannot reach your camera or location. If a site forgets, an embed might not work.
story.for_makers: Sites use it to lock off powerful features from third party frames, such as ads or widgets. It lowers the damage if an embed is hacked. Embedding services must also ask for the access they need through the allow attribute.

use_cases.example: A site embeds a video meeting in a frame and allows camera and microphone only for that frame.
A publisher blocks geolocation and camera for all ad frames so ads cannot reach them.
A game portal allows fullscreen and gamepad access only to the game frame.
A shop allows the payment request feature only for its payment provider frame.
A bank turns off camera, microphone and location for its own pages.
A team tests that a third party widget breaks cleanly when a feature is blocked.
A company web portal blocks sensors for all embedded dashboards.

risks: Only as safe as the site makes it

technical_bounds: Camera, microphone, geolocation default to self
Directive names vary per browser
Cannot grant what the user denied

capabilities.name: ASN, ISP and hosting type
capabilities.plain: The IP maps to an ISP or hosting company, which tells if the visitor is a home, mobile or cloud user.
capabilities.meaning: ASN databases label IPs as residential, mobile, business, hosting or education. Datacenter ASNs (AWS, GCP, OVH) trigger bot and fraud rules. Residential proxies are harder to spot.

story.what_it_is: Your internet address reveals whether you are on a home, phone or cloud network.
story.for_you: You never see this. Sites can tell if you are on a home internet plan, a mobile carrier, a school, a company or a cloud server. A VPN shows up as a hosting company.
story.for_makers: Fraud, ad and bot teams treat cloud and hosting addresses as higher risk. Streaming and gaming sites use it to spot VPNs and proxies, and ads use it to guess business or home.

use_cases.example: A game site blocks or flags accounts that come from cloud server addresses, which are common for bots.
A cloud gaming service checks that your network looks like home or mobile before it routes you to a nearby server.
A streaming service blocks known VPN hosting networks to enforce regional rights.
A ticket site slows down visitors from datacenters to stop scalper bots.
An ad network spots data center traffic and does not bill for it.
A bank adds risk when a login suddenly comes from a hosting provider.

technical_bounds: Labels lag behind IP leasing changes
Residential proxy networks defeat hosting checks

value.abuse: Network based profiling

marketing.name: Turnstile

marketing.pitch: Google describes risk scoring that decides if a visitor is human with little or no interaction.

story.for_makers: Makers fight fake accounts, scalpers, scraping and click fraud. They read browser quirks, network details and mouse patterns. This helps stop bots, but the same signals can also act as a fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A game login or shop uses a bot check so cheat sellers cannot mass create accounts.
An online ticket or loot drop page blocks bots so real players can buy limited items.
A sneaker or concert ticket sale blocks scalper bots at checkout.
An ad platform filters fake clicks so advertisers do not pay for bots.
A bank or login page scores each visit by browser, network and behavior before it asks for a password.

marketing.pitch: Chrome pitches it as a more private, structured replacement for the old user agent string, where sites ask for the details they need.

story.for_makers: Makers use hints to send the right images, files and layout for each device, which makes pages faster. Fraud and ad systems also use the detail as a fingerprint input, so what a server asks for matters.

A product team counts visitors by exact device model and system version.

capabilities.plain: Every request carries the sender's public IP address.
capabilities.meaning: The server sees the IP (or the proxy or relay address). IPv4 gives about 32 bits at most; an IPv6 /64 gives up to 64. It is the base for geolocation, ISP and VPN checks, and rate limits. Shared NAT and CGNAT blur it.

Be sure it is you; shared connections and carrier networks blur it

story.for_you: You never see it, but every site you visit receives your network address. It shows your internet provider and rough area. A VPN or relay swaps it for another address.
story.for_makers: Makers need it to send you the page. They also use it for rough location, rate limits, abuse blocking and fraud, and ads use it to link visits from the same home or office.

Learn your name from it

story.what_it_is: A page makes your browser look up odd web names so it can see which DNS service you use.
story.for_you: You see nothing. The page quietly asks your browser to look up random names, and the site's own server sees which DNS service asked. That can show your internet provider or whether a VPN is leaking.

use_cases.example: A VPN leak test website shows which DNS service your computer uses, and whether it matches the VPN.
A fraud system compares the DNS service with the claimed country and flags a mismatch.
A game anti cheat or region lock service checks whether a player behind a VPN is faking a region.

can: Hide the site name from your internet provider on supported sites
Hide your DNS lookups from your network with secure DNS
Keep working on supported sites without changing how pages look

Work in Safari today

story.what_it_is: Hides which site you connect to from people watching your network.

marketing.name: Encrypted Client Hello
marketing.pitch: Cloudflare pitches it as the missing piece that hides which website you visit from anyone watching the connection.

marketing.name: DNS over HTTPS
marketing.pitch: Mozilla describes DNS over HTTPS as a way to encrypt website lookups so others on the network cannot see them.

story.for_you: You see nothing change. On public Wi-Fi or at a school, the network can no longer easily see which site you are opening. Your home network or work can still see that you connected.
story.for_makers: Makers get stronger privacy for visitors and fewer blocked connections. Network filters, schools and countries lose an easy way to block sites by name. Some security tools also lose visibility.

use_cases.example: A news site in a country with censorship becomes harder for the network to block by name.
A gamer on school or hotel Wi-Fi opens a game site that the network blocks by name, and it still loads.

capabilities.meaning: Each bit is a subdomain set to HSTS or not. The tracker reads it back by probing http:// URLs and seeing which upgrade (Kamkar 2015). Safari's ITP and clearing site data restrict it; HSTS is mostly cleared with history.

web.api: Strict-Transport-Security on N subdomains; redirect probing

steps: Set HSTS on chosen subdomains to write bits
Check which redirect to https to read the ID

Recognise a returning visitor until you clear history or site data

story.what_it_is: A site stores an ID in which of its sub-sites your browser forces onto secure mode.
story.for_you: You never see it. Your browser remembers secure site choices. A tracker can set many tiny secure flags like switches and read them back later to see your personal code. Many browsers now limit this trick.
story.for_makers: It is an old trick to recognize people after cookie clearing, and it still shapes how browsers handle secure site lists. Trackers once used it. Privacy teams want it blocked.

use_cases.example: A tracker sets a pattern of secure site flags on a first visit and reads it back to recognize you.
An analytics vendor uses it as a backup ID when cookies are deleted.
A researcher shows how it could re identify private browsing users.
A store ad partner uses it to re identify a shopper who cleared cookies.
A publisher could match a returning reader behind a paywall.
A game site could link repeat sessions of a banned player.

technical_bounds: Needs dozens of subdomains and many requests
Cleared when the person clears browsing data

value.abuse: Cookie-free persistent ID

history.change: WebKit limits HSTS to prevent cross-site tracking (ITP)

capabilities.name: HTTP header order and casing
capabilities.plain: The set and order of request headers is different for each browser and HTTP library.
capabilities.meaning: Chrome, Firefox and Safari send Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding and Sec-* headers in distinct orders; scripted clients (requests, Go, Node fetch) differ. Mismatches versus the User-Agent flag bots.

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from the order of request headers
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens with every page request
can: Compare the order and casing of header lines with known browsers
Spot scripts and bots that use plain code libraries
Flag a browser name that does not match the headers
cannot: Know your name or account from it
See your files or other tabs
Tell two people on the same browser version apart

story.what_it_is: The order of the info your browser sends to a site reveals which browser it is.
story.for_you: You never see it. Each browser sends the same pieces in a slightly different order, like a signature. A site can tell Chrome from Firefox from a script even if the browser claims otherwise.
story.for_makers: Bot defense vendors use header order as a quick way to catch scripts pretending to be browsers. It is also a fingerprint input, since software versions and add-ons leave marks.

use_cases.example: A bot defense checks if the header order matches the browser claim, and blocks scripts that fake Chrome.
A game login page blocks credential stuffing tools that send headers in an odd order.
A sneaker or ticket site spots scalper bots by header order before the sale begins.
An ad platform filters click fraud from scripts with the wrong header signature.
A traffic report separates real browsers from crawlers.
A streaming site stops account sharing and scraping tools by headers.

technical_bounds: Proxies and CDNs can reorder headers
HTTP/2 lowercases names

value.abuse: Client identification

capabilities.name: HTTP/2 connection fingerprint (Akamai)
capabilities.plain: HTTP/2 settings, window updates and header order differ by browser and are readable by the server.
capabilities.meaning: Akamai's fingerprint (Black Hat EU 2017) joins SETTINGS values, WINDOW_UPDATE, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order. Chrome sends m,a,s,p, Firefox m,p,a,s and Safari m,s,p,a; Go and Python clients differ visibly.

web.api: HTTP/2 frame capture at the edge

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from how your connection starts up
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as your browser connects to the site
can: Compare connection settings and header order with known browsers
Tell Chrome, Firefox and Safari apart from each other
Spot scripts and bots whose settings look different
cannot: Know your name or account from it
Tell two people on the same browser apart
Apply to old HTTP/1.1 connections

story.what_it_is: The way your browser opens a modern web connection leaves a signature the site can read.
story.for_you: You never see it. When you connect, your browser sends settings in a pattern that is almost the same for every copy of Chrome, Safari or Firefox. A site can tell the real thing from a lookalike script.
story.for_makers: Security vendors like Akamai and Cloudflare use it to tell real browsers from bots that fake a browser name. It catches many scrapers and card testing tools. It also adds to a fingerprint that is hard to change.

use_cases.example: A bot defense compares the connection pattern with the claimed browser and challenges mismatches.
A retailer stops price scrapers that pretend to be Chrome.
A game launcher site blocks automated tools that buy limited items.
An ad platform removes fake traffic from automation tools.
A bank adds the connection pattern to its fraud score at login.
A traffic analyst uses it to name the real browser share.

technical_bounds: Spoofable by custom HTTP stacks
Same fingerprint across browser versions sharing an engine

value.abuse: Cross-session client identification

refs.label: Shuster et al., Passive Fingerprinting of HTTP/2 Clients (Black Hat EU 2017)

capabilities.name: HTTP/3 and QUIC fingerprint
capabilities.plain: QUIC's first packet carries a readable ClientHello, giving the same fingerprints as TLS plus transport parameters.
capabilities.meaning: The QUIC Initial packet is encrypted with a public key, so middleboxes can read the TLS ClientHello and QUIC transport parameters. JA4 has a QUIC variant (prefix q). Connection ID length and version also differ per stack.

web.api: QUIC Initial packet decrypt at edge; JA4 q variant

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from the first packet of a fast connection
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your browser opens a new HTTP/3 connection
can: Compare the opening packet and its settings with known browsers
Use the same kind of fingerprint as normal secure connections
Spot scripts and bots with unusual connection details
cannot: Know your name or account from it
Tell two people on the same browser apart
Apply to sites that do not use HTTP/3

story.what_it_is: The first packet of the newest connection type shows readable clues about your browser.
story.for_you: You never see it. When your browser starts a fast new type of connection, the first message has readable details that match your browser and system. A server can tell real browsers from fake ones.
story.for_makers: Bot defense and fraud teams extend their older checks to the newest connection type. It gives them the same browser signature plus extra transport details. It also adds to a long term fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A bot defense reads the first packet and blocks tools that fake a browser name.
A game portal blocks cheat sellers that script account creation.
A retailer protects limited drops from bots.
A video site blocks scrapers that rip its streams.
An ad network filters click farms by connection pattern.
A researcher measures which browsers use the new connection type.

technical_bounds: Less deployed than TCP fingerprints
ECH will hide inner ClientHello fields

value.abuse: Same as JA4

history.change: RFC 9000 and 9001 define QUIC and its TLS binding

capabilities.name: IP geolocation
capabilities.plain: The server converts the visitor's IP into an approximate country, region and city.
capabilities.meaning: Commercial databases (MaxMind, IPinfo, IP2Location) map IPs to places. Vendors claim about 99.8% country accuracy, but city accuracy is much lower and mobile or VPN IPs often point to the carrier hub or exit.

web.api: GeoIP lookup of the client IP (MaxMind GeoIP2, IPinfo)

steps: Query a local or API database
Return country, region, city, postal, lat and long

data.metric: Country, region, city, lat and long with accuracy radius

fields.name: accuracy radius
fields.precision: city level in good cases, vendor reported

limits.headline: Can guess your country, region and city from your IP address
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device connects to the site
can: Look up a likely country, region and city from your IP
Show local content, prices and language
Spot a mismatch with your time zone, such as when you use a VPN
cannot: Find your street or home; city guesses are much less exact than country
Get it right on mobile and VPN connections, which often point to a carrier hub or exit
Know your name or account from it
limits.reach_label: Country is close, city is rough

story.what_it_is: A site turns your internet address into a guess of your country, region and city.
story.for_you: You never have to allow anything. Sites guess your country and often your city from your internet address. It is right for countries most of the time, less for cities. A VPN changes the guess.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for local prices, language, taxes and rights. Ads use it for regional targeting. Fraud teams compare it with your billing address and sign in history.

use_cases.example: A game site picks your server region and shows local store prices.
A cloud gaming service uses it to see which data center is close to you and whether the game is licensed in your country.
A streaming service uses it to show only the shows allowed in your country.
A store shows prices, taxes and delivery for your country.
An ad network shows local ads for your city, such as nearby store offers.
A bank flags a login from a country the customer has never visited.
A site measures where its readers live without asking them.

technical_bounds: City accuracy varies widely and is often wrong for mobile and VPN users
Does not reveal street address

value.legit_uses: Content localization, tax and licensing, fraud rules
value.abuse: Price discrimination, geoblocking, stalking via leaked city

capabilities.name: IP masking (Private Relay, IP Protection, Tor)
capabilities.plain: Some browsers route traffic through relays so sites do not see the visitor's real IP.
capabilities.meaning: iCloud Private Relay (Safari, iCloud+ subscribers) uses two hops with a coarse egress location. Chrome IP Protection proxies selected third-party traffic in Incognito for known trackers. Tor routes everything over 3 hops.

web.api: OHTTP-style multi-hop relays; MASQUE; Tor circuits

steps: Browser sends traffic to a relay

chrome.note: :IP Protection for third-party traffic in Incognito (rolling out)

edge.note: :IP Protection for third-party traffic in Incognito (rolling out)

chrome_android.note: :IP Protection for third-party traffic in Incognito (rolling out)

samsung.note: :IP Protection for third-party traffic in Incognito (rolling out)

limits.headline: Can see only a relay's address when you browse with Private Relay, IP Protection or Tor
limits.user_action: You turn on iCloud Private Relay, use Tor Browser, or browse in Chrome Incognito with IP Protection
can: See the relay's internet address instead of your home address
Guess your rough area from the coarse location a relay shares
Treat relay traffic as higher risk and ask extra questions or block it
cannot: Learn your real home address when the relay is working
Tell that a relay is in use with certainty, since a site can only guess from known relay lists
Get this from Firefox, which has no built in relay feature
Break the relay for you; the protection stays on until you switch it off
limits.differs: Private Relay is Safari with iCloud+; IP Protection is limited to Chrome Incognito and known trackers; Firefox has no built in relay.

story.what_it_is: Some browsers and services hide your real internet address behind a relay so sites see a different one.

marketing.name: iCloud Private Relay
marketing.pitch: Sends your browsing through two relays so no single party knows both who you are and which sites you visit.

marketing.name: Tor Browser
marketing.pitch: Bounces your traffic through volunteer servers so websites cannot see where you really connect from.

story.for_you: You usually notice nothing. Pages load as normal, but a site may think you are in a nearby city, not your own. Some sites may ask extra questions or block you because your address looks hidden.
story.for_makers: Makers see the relay's address, not the visitor's home address. That breaks easy location guessing, ad targeting by address and per-person rate limits. Teams must decide whether to trust, challenge or block these visitors.

use_cases.example: A Safari user with Private Relay on opens a news site. The site sees a shared regional address, so it shows a broad local edition, not street level local ads.
A player in a browser shooter connects through a relay. The game server sees a relay address, so matchmaking picks a server by relay region and ping can rise a few milliseconds.

Cloud gaming in the browser, such as Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW, checks region before starting. A masked address can show the wrong country or add lag, so the player may be told the service is unavailable.
An ad network normally buys local ads by address. With masking, it only knows the broad area, so it falls back to page topic ads and reports less precise location data.
A bank sees a login from a relay address it has never seen. It may ask for a code by text, because relays hide the usual signals of where the person lives.
A store applies country pricing and tax by address. A masked visitor may see another region's price until they enter a shipping address at checkout.
A site counts unique visitors by address. Many people share one relay address, so the count is lower and the city report is blurrier.

technical_bounds: Only protects against sites, not the relay operator
Relay IPs appear on VPN lists and trigger blocks
Chrome IP Protection covers listed third-party domains only (reported)

value.abuse: Fraud and bot blockers treat relays as high risk

history.change: IP Protection roll out in Incognito (approximate, unverified)

capabilities.name: IPv6 prefix and interface ID stability
capabilities.plain: IPv6 addresses can stay stable for weeks, making them a long lived ID even if cookies are cleared.
capabilities.meaning: The /64 prefix delegated by an ISP often persists for weeks or months, while privacy extensions rotate the interface ID (about daily). Servers key on the /64 or /56 to identify a household.

limits.headline: Can tell your home network apart by its stable IPv6 address, even after clearing cookies
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device loads a page over IPv6
can: See the first half of your IPv6 address, which often stays the same for weeks or months
Recognize the same household again after you clear cookies
Use it to limit how many requests one home can make
cannot: Tell which person or device at home is browsing from the stable part alone
Follow you once you move to a different network, such as a cafe or mobile data
Follow the second half of the address for long, since devices change it about daily
Work for you if your connection is IPv4 only

story.what_it_is: Your IPv6 internet address can stay the same for weeks, so it can quietly work like a long lived ID.
story.for_you: You never see this. Your home network is given a long lasting address block, and every site you visit can see the same front part of it. Clearing cookies does not change it.
story.for_makers: Makers can link visits from the same home even when cookies are gone. It is cheap and works for every request. Privacy extensions rotate part of the address, but the network prefix often stays put.

use_cases.example: An ad network sees the same home network prefix across three different news sites. It treats the visits as one household and shows follow up ads even though cookies were cleared.
A shop's fraud system sees a new account come from the same IPv6 prefix as ten banned accounts. It holds the order for review.
A browser game bans a cheater by network prefix. The player who clears cookies and makes a new account still gets blocked because the prefix matches.
An analytics tool uses the prefix, plus browser clues, to stitch a repeat visitor across weeks when cookies are blocked.
A social site spots many fake accounts created from one household prefix and limits sign ups from it.
A streaming site limits how many devices can play at once per household and uses the network prefix to tell which devices share a home.
A company login portal trusts a staff member's home prefix as a familiar place, and asks for less proof from it.

technical_bounds: Privacy extensions rotate the interface ID, not the prefix
Mobile carriers change prefix more often

value.abuse: Household level tracking

refs.label: RFC 7721 Security and privacy of IPv6 addressing

capabilities.name: JA3 TLS client fingerprint
capabilities.plain: The TLS handshake order of ciphers and extensions identifies the client software.
capabilities.meaning: JA3 (Salesforce, 2017) is an MD5 of version, ciphers, extensions, curves and point formats in the ClientHello. Chrome 110 randomized extension order (Jan 2023), so one browser now yields many JA3s; JA4 sorts them out.

web.api: TLS ClientHello parsing at CDN or server

fields.name: ja3_hash
fields.precision: exact, but unstable on Chrome 110 and later

limits.headline: Can guess which browser or app you use from how your connection starts
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens the moment your browser connects to the site
can: Make a short code from the list of options your browser offers when it connects
Spot bots, scripts and malware that connect differently from real browsers
Recognize the same software again across different internet addresses
cannot: See your name, account or what you browse
Give one steady code for Chrome, since Chrome shuffles the order and gives many codes
Be turned off in your browser settings
Tell two people with identical software apart
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge shuffle the options on purpose, so one browser gives many codes. Firefox and Safari keep a steadier order.

story.what_it_is: The way your browser starts a secure connection leaves a pattern that names the software you use.
story.for_you: You never see it. Before any page loads, your browser says hello in a particular order. Servers can turn that order into a short code that points to your browser family.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to tell real Chrome or Safari apart from scripts and bots pretending to be them. It happens before any page code runs, so it is hard to fake. Browsers now shuffle the order, which weakens it.

use_cases.example: A ticket site gets a flood of requests that say they are Chrome. The secure handshake code matches a Python script, so the site blocks them before the sale opens.
An ad network checks that clicks come from real browsers. Clicks with a known bot handshake code are dropped and not billed to the advertiser.
A browser game's login server blocks a cheating tool that automates logins, because its handshake matches a known tool and not a normal browser.
A sneaker store uses the handshake code to spot buying bots that fake a browser name, so real shoppers get a fairer chance.
A bot defence service lists the most common handshake codes in its traffic and sets alarms when a rare one suddenly appears.
A bank's login page treats a handshake that does not match the claimed browser as a warning sign and adds a challenge.
A developer scraping a site with a plain script gets blocked, and learns the site compares the handshake code with the browser name sent.

technical_bounds: Chrome randomization makes the hash non-stable
Easy to spoof with curl-impersonate or uTLS

value.abuse: Persistent client identification across IPs

history.change: TLS extension order randomized, breaking static JA3 hashes

capabilities.name: JA4+ network fingerprint family
capabilities.plain: A newer family of fingerprints for TLS, HTTP, TCP and more, built to survive randomization.
capabilities.meaning: JA4 (FoxIO, 2023) sorts ciphers and extensions so Chrome's shuffle gives one value. JA4S (server), JA4H (HTTP), JA4L (latency), JA4X (cert), JA4SSH and JA4T (TCP) extend it. JA4 is BSD licensed; the rest use FoxIO License 1.1.

steps: Hash into a readable a_b_c string

limits.headline: Can recognize your browser or app from several quiet network clues, even when shuffled
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device connects and sends requests
can: Build a sorted code from how your browser starts a connection, so shuffling does not hide it
Add clues from the web request, connection timing and certificates
Use the codes to block bots and hunt for attacks
Keep tracking the same client across different internet addresses
cannot: See who you are by name or account
See page content or what you type
Be switched off from your browser settings
Tell apart two people with the same software and similar setup

story.what_it_is: A newer set of network fingerprints that still names your software, even when browsers shuffle their handshake.
story.for_you: You never see this. Many layers of your connection, from secure handshake to web request, leave small patterns. Together they point to what kind of device and software you use.
story.for_makers: Makers use these codes because they stay useful after browsers randomize order. Defenders share lists of good and bad codes to catch bots and malware. The same data can quietly help sort visitors without cookies.

use_cases.example: A bot defence service sees a login attack that claims to be Safari on iPhone. The network codes match a Linux scripting tool, so it blocks the traffic.
An ad exchange flags fake traffic farms because thousands of visits share one rare network code but claim to be many different phones.
A cloud gaming sign in page rejects automated account sellers whose connection pattern matches a known tool and not a real browser.
A ticket seller keeps a list of codes seen in past scalper attacks and rejects new requests that match them.
A company's security team uses the codes to spot a stolen login coming from a very different kind of device than the owner's laptop.
A threat research team groups web attacks by shared code to find which ones come from the same toolkit.
A bank adds the code to its risk score at login. A match with the customer's usual code lowers friction for them.

technical_bounds: Spoofable by uTLS and curl-impersonate
Software versions share hashes

value.legit_uses: Bot management, threat hunting (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Fastly)
value.abuse: Client tracking

history.change: JA4 and JA4+ announced by FoxIO
Cloudflare exposes JA4 in Bot Management

capabilities.name: Local Network Access (LNA) permission
capabilities.plain: Chrome asks the user before a public website can reach devices on their local network.
capabilities.meaning: Chrome 142 added a prompt for requests to private IPs. Chrome 145 split it into local-network and loopback-network permissions, and 147 extended it to WebSocket and WebTransport. It replaced Private Network Access preflights.

access.prompt_ui: Look for and connect to any device on your local network

limits.headline: Can connect to devices on your home network, only if you allow it in Chrome
limits.user_action: You open a site and tap Allow on Chrome's local network pop up
can: Look for and connect to printers, routers and smart home devices on your network once you allow it
Talk to local helper apps from a public website
Keep this access for the site until you take it back in site settings
cannot: Reach local devices before you tap Allow in Chrome 142 and newer
Work in Firefox or Safari, which do not offer this permission
Get around the pop up; the old silent checks were replaced by it
Reach your network from Chrome on iPhone
limits.differs: Only Chrome and Edge ask. Firefox, Safari and every iPhone browser do not offer this permission.

story.what_it_is: Chrome asks before a public website can talk to devices in your home or office network.

marketing.name: Local Network Access
marketing.pitch: Chrome now asks you first when a public website tries to reach devices on your local network, to stop sneaky probing.

story.for_you: A pop up asks if the site may look for and connect to devices on your local network. If you say no, the site cannot reach your printer, speakers or router. Nothing changes if you say no and do not need that device.
story.for_makers: Makers who build companion web apps for printers, smart speakers or developer tools must now ask first and explain why. It replaces older hidden checks with one clear permission. Sites that never ask lose silent access.

use_cases.example: A web dashboard for a smart home hub finds lights and thermostats on your network. Chrome asks first, then the page controls them from the browser.
A web player offers to send music to speakers in your living room. Chrome asks to find local devices before the speaker list shows up.
A developer opens a public docs site that talks to a tool running on their own network. They approve once so the page can reach it.
A company's cloud admin page connects to an office printer or card reader by its local address, after a one time allow.
A browser game party site lists consoles or PCs on your Wi-Fi so you can start streaming a game to the web page.
A web casting page searches for TVs on your network and asks first, then shows your nearby TVs.
A malicious ad tries to poke your router login. Chrome shows a prompt, which warns you that something odd is happening.

technical_bounds: Only Chromium; Firefox and Safari have no equivalent prompt
Users can accept for the site persistently

value.legit_uses: Local helper apps, smart home dashboards
value.abuse: Local device probing if granted

history.change: Split into local-network and loopback-network (secondary sources)
Extended to WebSocket and WebTransport (secondary sources)

capabilities.name: Localhost and LAN port scanning
capabilities.plain: A page probes ports on the visitor's own machine or home network to find running software.
capabilities.meaning: JavaScript uses fetch, WebSocket or image timing to test localhost ports (eBay's 2020 check, Meta Pixel and Yandex on Android in 2025 messaging via localhost). Chrome LNA prompts since 142 and PNA aim to stop this.

web.api: fetch/WebSocket/img to 127.0.0.1 and RFC1918 hosts; timing

limits.headline: Can try to find software running on your own computer, though Chrome now blocks it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page or ad script loads
can: Test whether your computer has certain programs listening, by timing quick requests
Check whether a companion desktop app is installed
Link web activity to an app on the same device
cannot: Do this silently in Chrome 142 and newer, which shows a pop up first
See files or data inside the programs it finds
Reach other devices on your network without the local network pop up
Work on iPhone browsers against apps, which are sandboxed from each other
limits.reach_label: Your own device, if not blocked
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge now ask first. Firefox and Safari still allow the quiet checks, though they only find what a site already expects. Android apps have been caught doing this.

story.what_it_is: A web page quietly checks which programs are running on your own computer or home network.
story.for_you: You never see it. A page you visit can try to connect to your own computer and learn which apps are open. The answer helps a site decide who you are.
story.for_makers: Some sites use it for fraud checks, such as spotting remote control software. Others have used it to collect hidden signals about the visitor. Browsers are adding rules to stop it.

use_cases.example: A bank site checks for common remote access tools on the visitor's machine. If one is running, it blocks the transfer to stop a scam call from taking over.
An ad script tests a list of local ports to build a hidden fingerprint of installed apps, which adds to a profile without cookies.
A browser game tries to connect to a helper app on a local port. If it answers, the game unlocks desktop features for that player.
A messaging web page checks a local port to see if the desktop app is running. If so, it opens chats there and not in the tab.
A developer tool in the browser connects to a helper on localhost to read files, so the site can show them in the page.
A fraud tool on a checkout page watches for debugging or automation tools open on the buyer's computer.
A company portal checks for its security agent on a local port before it lets staff sign in.

technical_bounds: Chrome 142 gates local requests behind a prompt
Firefox and Safari have no prompt yet (unverified at 2026-11)

value.abuse: Fraud detection by eBay, tracking ID bridging, router attacks

history.change: eBay port scanning reported by Nullsweep
