capabilities.name: Private Access Tokens and PACT
capabilities.plain: A signed token proves the visitor is probably a real device without revealing who they are.
capabilities.meaning: Privacy Pass (RFC 9576 to 9578) tokens issued after device or account attestation. Apple PAT ships in Safari and Cloudflare Turnstile consumes tokens. PACT was announced on 2026-06-22 by Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and Shopify; Apple was not listed.

web.api: Privacy Pass PrivateToken challenge in WWW-Authenticate; PAT

safari.note: Private Access Tokens for iOS 16 and macOS 13

limits.headline: Can check that you are probably a real device without learning who you are
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a site asks your browser to prove it is genuine
can: Receive a signed token showing a real Apple device or account vouched for you
Skip a CAPTCHA or other challenge for you
Accept the same token without knowing which device made it
cannot: Learn your name, device model or account from the token
Track you from token to token, since they are made to be unlinkable
Work in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Samsung Internet today
Prove you are human with certainty, only that a trusted device vouched
limits.differs: Only Safari on Mac and iPhone issues these tokens today. A cross vendor version called PACT was announced in June 2026.

story.what_it_is: A signed token that proves you are probably a real device, without telling the site who you are.

marketing.name: Private Access Tokens
marketing.pitch: Lets sites skip CAPTCHAs by checking quietly that a real Apple device is visiting, without learning who you are.

marketing.name: Private Access Tokens
marketing.pitch: Cloudflare says these tokens remove CAPTCHAs on iPhones and Macs while keeping visitors private.

story.for_you: On supported Apple devices you see fewer puzzles asking you to pick traffic lights. Your phone proves itself in the background. You never see the check.
story.for_makers: Makers get a strong sign that the visitor is a real device, and not a bot farm, with no extra data to store. It cuts fraud and friction. Sites need a provider such as Cloudflare to issue and check tokens.

use_cases.example: A shop behind Cloudflare skips the puzzle for iPhone shoppers, so more people finish checkout and bots still have to solve harder tests.
A browser game's sign up page checks for a real device token, so one person cannot make hundreds of free accounts for cheating.
A social site lets verified devices post and follow right away, and challenges unverified ones with extra steps.
An ad network discounts clicks that come without a token on devices that normally have one, which reduces click fraud.
A login page uses the token to lower friction for real devices and raise it for scripts that try thousands of passwords.
A news site limits scraping by asking for a token before it serves full articles to automated visitors.
A person who finds image puzzles hard to solve gets in with no puzzle, because the device proves itself in the background.

technical_bounds: Issuers can see attestation requests; issuer collusion is the main risk
PACT is only announced; shipping status unverified

value.abuse: Attestation could exclude minority browsers or devices

history.change: RFC 9576 to 9578 Privacy Pass published (Jun 2024 per IETF)
PACT announced by Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, Shopify

capabilities.name: Referer and Origin headers
capabilities.plain: Requests tell the destination site which page the visitor came from.
capabilities.meaning: The default policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin (Chrome 85, Firefox 87) sends only the origin cross-site. Safari has capped cross-site referrers to the origin since 12.1. Full URLs still go same-site.

web.api: Referer and Origin request headers; Referrer-Policy; document.referrer

limits.headline: Can tell which site you came from, usually just the site name, not the page
limits.user_action: You click a link or load a page that pulls in another site's content
can: See the site address you arrived from, such as example.com
See the full page address when you move around inside the same site
Count visits by traffic source for analytics
cannot: See the full page address of another site you left, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari by default
See your browsing history beyond the one step before
Get a referrer if the previous page chose to send none
limits.reach_label: One step back, mostly the site name
limits.differs: Safari has limited cross site referrers to the site name for years. Chrome and Firefox did the same by default around 2020 and 2021.

story.what_it_is: Each request tells the destination which page or site you came from.

marketing.name: Referrer Policy
marketing.pitch: The standard lets sites choose how much of the previous page address is shared when you click a link.

story.for_you: You never see it. When you click a link or a page loads an image, the other site learns where you were. Browsers now trim it to just the site name by default, so you share less than before.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to see which sites and ads send visitors, to block other sites from copying their images, and to guard forms from forged requests. The origin header helps stop cross site attacks.

use_cases.example: A shop sees that many visitors arrive from a blog post. The referrer tells it which blog to thank and which affiliate to pay.
An advertiser reads the referrer to check that clicks came from the sites it paid, and to spot fake sites.
A photo site stops other sites from showing its pictures for free by checking the referrer on image requests.
A banking site checks the origin header on a transfer form. A request coming from another site is rejected as forged.
A browser game portal sees which partner site a player came from, so it can credit the partner and show a matching start screen.
A social site shows a link preview but trims the referrer so private page addresses do not leak to the linked site.
A news site sees visitors from search, social and email, and uses it to pick which subscription offer to show.

technical_bounds: Pages can loosen it with Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url
Never reveals the referring page across origins by default

value.abuse: Leaks of sensitive URLs, search terms

capabilities.name: Reverse DNS (PTR) of the client IP
capabilities.plain: A reverse lookup of the IP can return an ISP hostname that hints at location or line type.
capabilities.meaning: PTR records such as pool-1-2-3-4.nycmny.fios.verizon.net expose ISP, city codes and sometimes dynamic vs static addressing. Servers do this for logs and bot checks (Googlebot verification).

web.api: DNS PTR lookup for in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa

limits.headline: Can look up your internet address to learn your provider and sometimes your area
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the site's server logs or checks your visit
can: Learn the name your internet provider gave your address
Spot city codes or home versus business lines in that name
Confirm that a visitor claiming to be a search crawler really is one
cannot: Learn your street address or your name
Work when your provider gives no useful name
See through a VPN or relay, which show their own names
Be blocked from your browser, since it happens on the server side

story.what_it_is: A lookup of your internet address can return a name hinting where you are or what line you use.
story.for_you: You never see it. The server may turn your numeric address into a name like a phone company or a school. That name hints at your area or whether you are on a home line or a data center.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to check that crawlers are who they say, to tell home users from servers, and to guess city or company. It is quick, free and needs no cooperation from the browser.

use_cases.example: A site that gets traffic claiming to be Googlebot checks the address name. If it does not end in Google's domain, it is blocked as an impostor.
An ad network uses the name to tell data center traffic from home traffic, and treats data center clicks as likely fake.
An analytics tool shows visits by company name, because staff of a firm browse from an address that names it.
A B2B sales tool spots a visit from a target company and alerts the salesperson.
A game server list blocks cloud hosting names for ranked play, to stop cheat servers and bots.
A video site sees a university address name and offers the campus subscription deal.
A mail or web server logs address names so staff can trace an abuse complaint to the right network owner.

technical_bounds: Many IPs have no PTR
Cloud IPs return generic names

value.abuse: Residential identification

capabilities.name: Sec-CH-UA low entropy hints and reduced User-Agent
capabilities.plain: Chromium sends brand, mobile flag and platform in every request by default, with a frozen User-Agent string.
capabilities.meaning: Sec-CH-UA lists browser brands and major versions (with a GREASE brand), Sec-CH-UA-Mobile and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. The User-Agent string is frozen to a reduced form in Chrome 110 and later.

web.api: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile, Sec-CH-UA-Platform request headers; navigator.userAgentData

limits.headline: Can see your browser brand, major version, phone or computer type, and system in Chromium browsers
limits.user_action: Nothing. Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet send it with every request
can: See your browser brand and its main version number
Tell if you are on a phone or a computer
See your operating system name
Ask for more detail such as exact version or device model, which the browser may then share
cannot: See your exact device model or full version unless it asks and the browser agrees
Get this from Firefox or Safari, which do not send it
See your name or account
Rely on the older browser name string, which is now kept short and generic
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet send it by default. Firefox and Safari, including all iPhone browsers, do not.

story.what_it_is: Chrome based browsers tell every site your browser brand, whether you are on mobile, and your system type.

marketing.name: User-Agent Client Hints
marketing.pitch: Chrome freezes the old browser string and shares details only when a site asks, to cut passive tracking.

story.for_you: You never see it. Each page request includes a short note: your browser brand, if it is a phone, and your platform. A site asks for more detail, such as device model, only if it needs it.
story.for_makers: Makers use the basic note to serve the right layout, the right app download link and the right video format. The old long browser string is frozen, so finer detail needs an extra request, which browsers can limit.

use_cases.example: A video site reads the platform and mobile flag and offers a phone friendly player without any page code running first.
A browser game portal sees you are on a phone and loads touch controls and a lighter graphics build.
An ad network picks banner sizes that fit mobile or desktop, and filters traffic whose claimed browser does not match its hints.
A store shows a link to its Android app on Android and its iPhone app on iOS using the platform hint.
A dashboard counts visits by browser brand and system without relying on the old, hard to read string.
A login system notes the brand and platform of a trusted device, and flags a sudden change as suspicious.
A developer decides which older browsers to still support by reading hint counts from live traffic.

technical_bounds: Platform string quantized, GREASE brand randomizes order
Firefox and Safari do not send it

value.abuse: Browser and OS identification

capabilities.name: Sec-Fetch-* request metadata
capabilities.plain: Browsers add headers saying where a request came from and why, which servers use to block cross-site abuse.
capabilities.meaning: Sec-Fetch-Site, Mode, Dest and User tell the server if a request is same-origin, a navigation, or user triggered. They are not user identifying but help servers tell real browsers from scripts.

limits.headline: Can tell why a request was sent, such as a click or a script
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser adds it to every request automatically
can: See whether a request came from the same site, another site, or from you directly
See whether it came from a click, a typed address or a page script
Block suspicious cross site requests and bots that lack the right labels
cannot: See your name, location or account from these labels
Be changed by the page, since the browser sets them
Tell which person you are
Learn which other pages you visited

story.what_it_is: Browsers label each request with where it came from and why, so servers can reject cross site abuse.

marketing.name: Fetch Metadata
marketing.pitch: Servers can use these labels to block requests that are not meant for them, as a defence against many web attacks.

story.for_you: You never see these labels, but they help protect you. They let sites refuse a request that a hostile page secretly sent using your logged in session.
story.for_makers: Makers add a short rule on the server: only accept some requests from their own pages. It blocks forged requests and data leaks across sites. Because browsers set the labels, a page cannot fake them.

use_cases.example: A bank's server refuses a money transfer sent by another site, because the label says it came from a different site and was not a normal navigation.
A social site only returns private profile data to requests from its own pages, so other sites cannot read it through hidden calls.
A browser game's account server rejects score submissions that do not come from its own game page, which cuts simple cheating by third party scripts.
A web editor such as Google Docs protects document data so other sites cannot load it into a hidden frame.
A streaming site blocks other sites from embedding its video files by checking the destination label.
An engineer adds a middleware that drops cross site requests to private APIs, then watches the logs for blocked probes.
A security team uses the labels to spot probing from a malicious page in the access logs.

technical_bounds: Absent from non-browser clients, making them a bot signal
Cannot be set by page script

value.legit_uses: CSRF and XSSI defense (resource isolation policies)
value.abuse: Bot detection

capabilities.name: TCP/IP passive OS fingerprint (p0f, JA4T)
capabilities.plain: The TCP handshake reveals the operating system through TTL, window size, MSS and option order.
capabilities.meaning: p0f (Zalewski) and JA4T read SYN fields: initial TTL (64 or 128), window size, MSS, window scale and option order. Windows, Linux, iOS and macOS differ, and a mismatch with the User-Agent signals spoofing or a proxy.

web.api: SYN packet capture (p0f v3, JA4T, Zeek)

limits.headline: Can guess your operating system from how your device opens a connection
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device first connects to the server
can: Guess whether you run Windows, Mac, Linux, Android or iPhone from connection details
Catch visitors whose claimed system does not match their real one
Filter attack traffic that has odd connection patterns
cannot: See your name, account or files
Tell the exact version or device model
Be hidden by clearing cookies or using private browsing
Work well through a proxy or relay, since it only sees the last hop

story.what_it_is: The very first network packets from your device reveal what kind of operating system it runs.
story.for_you: You never see it. Every device opens a connection in a slightly different way. A server can read that pattern and guess if you are on Windows, Mac, Linux or a phone.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to catch visitors who say one thing and are another, such as a bot claiming to be an iPhone while running on Linux. It needs no code in the browser and cannot be changed by a page.

use_cases.example: A ticket site sees a visitor claiming to be an iPhone, but the connection pattern looks like a Linux server. It blocks the request as a bot.
An ad fraud service compares the claimed device with the network pattern and drops mismatches from billing.
A browser game blocks sign ups from servers pretending to be Windows players, which stops bot farms and cheat tools.
A bank compares the system seen at login with the customer's usual one and asks for more proof if it changes.
A traffic report separates real phone visits from automated ones that spoof phone browsers.
A firewall flags an unexpected system type on a company login and steps up checks.
A retailer ties repeated suspicious orders to the same network pattern, and slows them for review.

technical_bounds: Altered by load balancers, VPNs and proxies
Reveals the network stack, not the browser

value.legit_uses: OS vs User-Agent mismatch detection, DDoS filtering
value.abuse: Silent OS identification

capabilities.name: TLS session resumption tracking
capabilities.plain: Reuse of a TLS session ticket can link a visitor's connections across sites that share a server.
capabilities.meaning: A session ticket or PSK is a stable ID, so two domains behind one CDN or server can see the same resumption. Sy et al. (ACSAC 2018) found browsers reusing tickets across origins. Chrome partitioned TLS session caches by network isolation key.

web.api: TLS 1.2 session tickets, TLS 1.3 PSK; session ID

limits.headline: Can link your visits across sites on one server if your browser reuses a ticket
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you return to a site and the connection resumes
can: See the same resume ticket when you visit two sites behind one server or content network
Use the ticket as a temporary ID to connect those visits
Speed up your next connection, which is the real purpose
cannot: Link visits on servers that do not share infrastructure
Keep the link for long, since tickets expire in hours or days
Work against browsers that keep separate tickets per site, such as Chrome and Firefox
See your name or what you do on the site
limits.differs: Chrome and Firefox keep tickets separate per site. Safari is partly protected. Older tests showed browsers reusing tickets across sites.

story.what_it_is: Reusing a saved secure connection ticket can link your visits across sites that share a server.
story.for_you: You never see it. To start faster, your browser reuses a ticket from an earlier secure connection. A server that sees the same ticket from two places can tell they are the same browser.
story.for_makers: Makers who run many sites on one server or provider can link visits without cookies. It is a quiet side effect of speed tricks. Browsers cut it by limiting how long tickets live and by splitting them per site.

use_cases.example: A big ad and content network serving many sites sees the same ticket on each. It joins the visits into one profile even with cookies blocked.
A hosting provider counts a returning visitor across all customer sites using the same ticket.
A defence service ties a bot's repeated requests to one ticket and blocks it, even if the address changes.
A video platform links a viewer across its sites and its player embeds through one reused connection.
A game portal hosting many titles on one server links a player's visits across games without a login.
A share button provider sees the same ticket on every site that embeds its button.
A privacy researcher tests whether a browser reuses tickets across sites, to see if it leaks.

technical_bounds: Ticket lifetime limited by browser (about 24 hours to 7 days)
Cross-site linking blocked by partitioning

value.abuse: Cross-domain linkage behind shared infrastructure

history.change: Sy et al. Tracking Users across the Web via TLS Session Resumption (ACSAC 2018)
TLS session cache partitioned with Network Isolation Key

refs.label: Sy et al., Tracking Users across the Web via TLS Session Resumption (ACSAC 2018)

capabilities.name: VPN, proxy and Tor detection
capabilities.plain: Sites guess whether the visitor hides behind a VPN, proxy or Tor.
capabilities.meaning: Methods: IP lists (Tor exit list, hosting ASNs), latency versus claimed geography, timezone and language versus IP, WebRTC leaks, open ports, MTU and TCP quirks. Residential VPN IPs often slip through.

web.api: IP reputation; Tor bulk exit list; RTT triangulation; timezone mismatch

steps: Compare IP geo with timezone and Accept-Language
Measure latency and run WebRTC probe

fields.name: is_vpn
fields.precision: vendor score, false positives about 1 to 10%

limits.headline: Can guess whether you are hiding behind a VPN, proxy or Tor, but not always correctly
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you load a page, sign in, or watch video
can: Check your address against lists of VPN, hosting and Tor addresses
Compare your timezone and language with where your address seems to be
Spot slow response times that suggest a faraway server
Block or challenge you, or show a different catalog
cannot: Be sure when you use a home internet VPN address, which often slips through
Learn your real address if the VPN holds up
See your name or account from detection alone
Avoid wrongly flagging people who use privacy tools for safety

story.what_it_is: Sites guess if you are hiding behind a VPN, proxy or Tor, using address lists and timing clues.
story.for_you: You may see a block page, a missing video or extra checks, and no clear reason. The site thinks your address belongs to a VPN, a data center or Tor, so it treats you with caution.
story.for_makers: Makers buy lists of VPN, proxy and Tor addresses to enforce region rules, stop fraud and slow bots. It is a blunt tool. It also catches honest people who use a VPN for privacy.

use_cases.example: Streaming sites such as Netflix and BBC iPlayer block known VPN addresses to enforce regional licenses, so a viewer abroad sees a proxy error.
A game's store checks for VPN use at purchase to stop regional price tricks, and may ask for a card from the local country.
A bank asks for extra proof when a login arrives from Tor or a known proxy, which may lock out a traveler.
A checkout page scores VPN traffic as higher risk and holds the first order for review.
An ad network refuses to bill clicks from data center and proxy addresses, because they are mostly bots.
A social site restricts new accounts from Tor to slow spam, though a journalist in a risky country may need Tor.
A ticket queue blocks proxy addresses so one buyer cannot hold many places in line.

technical_bounds: False positives on corporate and school networks
Residential proxies and private relays are hard to flag

value.abuse: Blocking privacy users, discrimination

capabilities.name: WebRTC ICE host candidates (mDNS)
capabilities.plain: WebRTC used to expose the device's local network IP; browsers now hide it behind a random .local name.
capabilities.meaning: RTCPeerConnection gathers ICE host candidates. Since 2019 and 2020 Chrome and Firefox replace private IPs with mDNS .local names, but granting getUserMedia (camera or microphone) restores real addresses.

fields.name: host candidate
fields.precision: hidden by default in modern browsers

limits.headline: Can try to find your device's home network address, but browsers now hide it
limits.user_action: You join a video call or visit a site that sets up a call connection
can: Start a call connection that lists your device's network addresses
See a random .local name in place of your real home network address in Chrome and Firefox
See your real home network address if you have also allowed camera or microphone
cannot: See your real home network address by default in Chrome and Firefox since 2019 and 2020
Set this up without a site script running
See other devices on your network from this alone
Be sure to bypass a VPN, since modern browsers mask the address
limits.differs: Chrome and Firefox hide the address by default. Safari asks differently and also shows a masked name unless camera or microphone is allowed.

story.what_it_is: Video call tech used to show your device's home network address. Browsers now hide it behind a random name.

marketing.name: mDNS ICE candidates
marketing.pitch: Browsers swap your local address for a random .local name, so calls still connect but the real address stays private.

story.for_you: On a video call or a multiplayer game you notice nothing. Behind the scenes your browser offers a random name instead of your home network address. Calls still work.
story.for_makers: Makers need these candidate addresses to link two devices directly, which cuts server cost and delay. Hiding the real address stops sites from quietly reading it, but direct links on the same network still work.

use_cases.example: Two coworkers on the same office Wi-Fi join a Google Meet call. Their browsers swap random local names and connect straight to each other, which keeps audio crisp.
A browser party game uses peer to peer data channels. Players on the same Wi-Fi link directly through hidden local names, so moves arrive with low delay.
A cloud gaming stream in a browser sets up a direct media path from the game server to the player. Hidden local names stop the page leaking the player's network layout.
A web chat app starts a voice room. Friends on one network connect with each other without sending audio through the company's servers.
A tracking script used to read local addresses to tell devices apart. With hidden names it gets a random value that changes, so that trick stops working.
A telehealth site lets a doctor and patient talk. It keeps the call direct when possible and avoids storing home addresses in logs.
A virtual classroom opens small group rooms. Students in the same school building connect over the local network, so lessons run smoothly.

technical_bounds: getUserMedia permission re-exposes local IPs
Still leaks IPv6 addresses in some cases

value.abuse: VPN bypass detection and local IP leak, LAN inventory

WebRTC leak popularized by VPN leak tests

capabilities.plain: A STUN request lets a page discover the public IP of the real network path, even behind some VPNs.

limits.headline: Can find the public internet address of your real connection, even when some VPNs hide it
limits.user_action: Nothing. A page can start a call setup without any pop up

story.for_you: You never see it. A page can start a hidden call setup and learn the public address your device really uses. If your VPN only covers some traffic, your real address may leak.
story.for_makers: Makers need this step so calls and games can connect through home routers. It is also used by fraud tools to see past proxies. Privacy tools block or limit it, which can break calls.

use_cases.example: Zoom or Google Meet in the browser asks a helper server what public address you appear to have, then shares it so the other person can reach you directly.
A browser multiplayer game with direct player links uses it so two players behind home routers can connect, without paying for a relay.
A bank's fraud script sets up a hidden call to learn the real address behind a VPN, and flags a mismatch with the connection address.
An ad tech script reads the real public address behind a proxy to catch click fraud from hidden networks.
A cloud gaming site uses it to pick the closest game server and the best path for the live video stream.
A fraud tool at checkout compares the address from the call setup with the address on the page request. Different values raise the risk score.
A developer opens browser leak test pages to check if their VPN hides the real address during calls.

Chrome policy setting disable_non_proxied_udp restricts it

capabilities.plain: Reads estimated connection speed, type and latency.

limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads and while you stay on it
can: Check if your connection looks like Wi-Fi, cellular or slow
See rough speed and delay figures, rounded in coarse steps
Notice when your connection changes and use it to link short visits
Load lighter pages when your link is slow
cannot: See your exact speed or your provider
Work in Firefox or Safari, which do not offer it
See your name or location from this alone
Tell Wi-Fi from cellular in most cases outside Android

story.what_it_is: A page can read how fast and stable your connection seems to be, like Wi-Fi or slow 4G.

marketing.pitch: Pages can adapt to a slow or fast connection by reading its estimated type, speed and delay.

story.for_makers: Makers use it to adjust quality, skip heavy features and measure real world speeds across customers. The same numbers add a small clue to a browser fingerprint. Only Chromium browsers share them.

use_cases.example: A streaming site starts a video at lower quality when the reported speed is poor, so the first frame shows quickly instead of a spinner.
A browser 3D game picks smaller textures and fewer effects on a slow connection, so a player on a train can still load the level.
A store sends lighter product pictures to shoppers on slow mobile data, which keeps them from leaving before the page loads.
A performance dashboard groups page speed by reported connection type, to show how real customers on 3G and Wi-Fi are doing.
A news site turns off auto loading videos on slow lines to keep articles readable.
A web design tool such as Figma pauses background downloads of large files when the connection looks weak.
An ad script uses the connection type and speed with other values to build a fingerprint of a device.

Not in Safari or Firefox

See if you prefer dark mode
Pick the right image size and theme before the page shows

See your name or account
Learn exact memory, since it is rounded

story.what_it_is: Browsers can send screen density, window size and memory with each page request when a site asks.

marketing.pitch: Servers can opt in to receive details about the device, so they can send the best version of a page first time.

use_cases.example: A store gets the screen sharpness and window width, then sends one right sized product photo, so a phone does not download a huge desktop image.
A browser game portal reads device memory and sends a lighter build to low memory phones, so the game does not crash on load.
A news site picks a dark or light page from the color scheme hint and avoids a bright flash on first paint.
A video site picks a starting quality from window width and screen sharpness before the player even loads.
An ad server picks an ad size matching the window width, and may combine other hints to recognize a device again.
A tool records memory and screen hints to show what kind of devices visitors use, and to plan support.
A developer tests a site on a low memory phone to see that the lighter version really arrives.

A web app sets up a smart light or printer by talking to its local network service directly.
A web app for music studios sends live note data to other devices on the same network using raw network messages.
A web based network tool scans office devices to find which are online, which is only allowed in an installed trusted app.

story.what_it_is: Servers can receive a note about your connection type, delay and speed with each request.

marketing.name: ECT header
marketing.pitch: Tells the server the browser's effective connection type, so it can pick lighter or richer content.

story.for_you: You never see it. If a site asks, your browser tells its server how good the connection seems. The server may send a smaller page if the line is slow.
story.for_makers: Makers can decide what to send before the browser runs any script. That saves time for slow users. The details also add a small clue to a device fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A video platform reads the hint on the first request and picks a lower starting quality for slow connections.
A store sends a short list of products with small pictures on slow lines, and the full page on fast ones.
A news site serves a text first version on slow connections, and loads pictures later.
A browser game site serves a smaller loader and delays heavy assets for players on slow lines.
An ad server picks a lightweight ad for slow connections so the page is not blocked.
A speed monitoring tool groups real page load times by connection type from the headers.
A government site gives a plain, light page to people on slow rural internet, so forms still work.

story.what_it_is: Your browser asks if a website may talk to devices on your home or office network.

marketing.name: Local Network Access
marketing.pitch: Chrome asks first when a public site wants to reach devices on your local network, to prevent hidden attacks on home gear.

story.for_you: A prompt asks if the site may look for and connect to devices on your network. Allow it only for sites you trust and need it for, like a printer setup page. Choosing block keeps your devices hidden.
story.for_makers: Makers of devices with web setup pages and cloud dashboards must ask. It is a clear moment to explain why access is needed. Sites that scan without a reason get blocked and lose trust.

use_cases.example: A thermostat's website asks to find the device on your Wi-Fi, so setup finishes in the browser with no app.
A web remote for a speaker asks to find speakers at home, then plays your playlist on them.
A web streaming page for a home gaming PC asks to find the PC on your network, and then starts a low delay stream.
A company's cloud print portal finds a printer on the office network after one allow.
A browser based dev tool reaches a test device on the lab network for debugging.
A shady page tries to reach your router's admin page. The browser prompt warns you and you can say no.
A web casting page looks for TVs on your Wi-Fi so you can send a video to the big screen.

technical_bounds: Applies to secure and mixed contexts
Does not cover navigations, only subresources

abuse: LAN scanning and router attacks from a webpage

A company portal checks for its endpoint security agent on this computer before login, with your permission.

story.what_it_is: A page can read your estimated connection type, speed and delay, and if data saver is on.

marketing.name: Network Information API
marketing.pitch: Lets pages adapt to the connection, such as sending less data on slow links or when data saver is on.

story.for_you: You never see a prompt. Sites may load lighter pictures or skip auto video if your line is slow or you turned on data saver. You just see a faster page.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to cut load time, save mobile data and keep users from leaving. It is also quietly counted in some fingerprints. Firefox and Safari do not offer it.

use_cases.example: A video site starts at 480p on a weak connection and moves up when speed improves.
A browser game checks speed before loading its big level pack and offers a smaller pack on slow lines.
A store shows tiny image placeholders first for shoppers with data saver on.
A news site holds back auto play video on slow connections and metered data plans.
A web editor such as Google Docs delays syncing big attachments until the connection is better.
A speed dashboard shows how page load changes by connection type across real visitors.
An ad script reads type, speed and delay as part of a device fingerprint.

technical_bounds: Chromium only

Cannot read Wi-Fi name or signal

marketing.pitch: Pages can react when the device goes offline or comes back, for example to save work for later.

story.for_you: You may see a banner like You are offline, or a message that your changes will sync later. When the signal returns, the page catches up for you.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to protect user work, to switch to a saved copy and to retry actions. It is a simple signal, but it can be wrong, as a device can look online with no real internet.

use_cases.example: Google Docs shows Offline in the top bar when your signal drops, keeps your typing and syncs when you reconnect.
A browser game pauses and shows Reconnecting when the signal drops, then rejoins the match when it returns.
A web streaming app switches to downloaded titles when it sees the device is offline.
A chat site shows a clock icon on unsent messages while offline and sends them when back online.
A shop keeps a cart on the device when offline and syncs it when online.
A web design tool like Figma warns that edits are saved on this device only until a connection returns.
A news site shows saved articles while you ride through a tunnel.

story.for_makers: Makers use it to cut costs and speed up pages for people on limited data. It is easy to support. It also tells the server a small thing about a user, which can add to a fingerprint.

A store shows fewer product photos on first load for shoppers who ask to save data.
A browser game portal delays the loading of trailers and keeps only the playable game for users who save data.
A social site skips auto playing clips in the feed for people with Data Saver.
A learning platform sends lighter lessons to students on limited mobile plans.
An ad server serves a lighter ad format when the header is on, so the page loads in time.

story.for_makers: Makers need these addresses to connect calls and games directly. Tracking and fraud scripts also read them to see past some VPNs. Privacy settings can block this, but may break calls.

use_cases.example: Browser video calls such as Google Meet gather addresses so your computer and the other person's can connect directly.

A tracking script reads the addresses to tell devices apart, a trick browsers now limit.
A web voice chat joins a room and shares your path with friends so audio stays low delay.
A developer uses a leak test page to check what a site can learn through calls.

story.for_you: Your saved sites stay between you and your browser. A web page has no way to look at them. Only a browser extension you install and allow can.

story.what_it_is: Sites cannot read which other sites you have visited.

marketing.name: Plugging the CSS history leak

story.for_you: Other websites cannot see where else you have been. Links you visited may be a different color, but sites cannot read that color. Your history stays with you.
story.for_makers: History is the richest ad and profiling data there is, so many tried to sniff it using link colors. Browsers closed the trick years ago. Sites now rely on cookies, logins, timing tricks and their own logs for the same kind of insight.

use_cases.example: An ad network wanted to know if you visited a rival store and now uses cookies on its own network instead.
A phishing site used to check which bank sites you visited, which no longer works.
A retailer wanted to know which competitors you checked and tracks its own visits only.

A game portal wanted to recommend games from your history, and only uses what you play on it.
A researcher showed that cache timing can hint at visited sites, which is why browsers now split caches by site.
A bank wanted to learn which other banks you use and cannot.

story.for_you: A website cannot copy your whole address book. On supported Android Chrome, a picker lets you tick a few people to share. Nothing else goes through.
story.for_makers: Apps want contact lists to grow quickly by inviting friends and matching people. The web picker gives only the ticked names each time. Native apps can take the whole list, which is why apps are in the news for it.

A web chat app wants to invite someone and lets you pick one contact.
A money app on the web lets you pick a friend to pay instead of sharing all contacts.
A ride site lets you pick a contact to share a trip with.
A dating site wanted to hide your profile from your contacts, which needs the full list and is not possible on the web.
A gift site wanted birthdays from contacts and uses the picker for one person.
An advertiser wanted contact lists for matching, which the web does not allow.

risks: You can still pick too many

technical_bounds: Social graph exposure

legit_uses: None: the browser deliberately withholds it

marketing.pitch: Google explains how a web app can ask to keep its data safe from cleanup.

story.for_makers: It protects work that is only on the device, like drafts, saves and offline files. Makers ask when losing data would hurt trust. The browser may decline.

use_cases.example: A browser game asks to protect your save file so you do not lose hours of play.
A note taking app asks to keep your offline notes before they sync.
A web design or music tool asks to keep a long local project.
A web music or reading app asks to keep your downloaded content.
A field work app asks to protect forms filled out without a signal.
A health diary web app asks to keep entries safe on your device.

story.for_you: You are never asked and never see it. A site can notice that private mode saves less data, and may then change what it shows you.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to enforce paywalls, spot fraud and avoid broken sites. Some publishers hide articles or ask people to log in. Privacy groups say this penalises people who want privacy.

use_cases.example: A news site notices private mode and blocks the free article count, asking you to sign in.
A bank or fraud service treats a private mode login as a little riskier and may add a code step.
An ad network sees private mode and does not store a profile ID for this visit.
A browser game warns that your progress cannot be saved in private mode.
A store warns that the cart will vanish when you close the private window.
A site team counts private mode visits to understand how many are missing from stats.

story.what_it_is: A store of up to about 5 MB for one tab that is cleared when you close the tab.

marketing.name: Window.sessionStorage
marketing.pitch: Documents how a page can keep data for the life of one tab.

story.for_you: You never see it. It is why a form can hold what you typed while you click through the steps, and why a new tab starts fresh.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for short lived state like multi step forms and temporary tokens. It is safer than long term storage, because it disappears with the tab. It is also used for session IDs in analytics.

A site analytics script uses it to mark one visit as one session.
An online test keeps your answers in the tab until you submit.

story.for_you: You never see it. It is why a chat site can keep one live connection for all your open tabs, saving battery and data.

A web app does one background sync for all open tabs of a document.

story.what_it_is: Lets an embedded third party frame ask for its own cookies back.

marketing.pitch: Documents how an embedded site can ask the browser for access to its own cookies.

story.for_makers: It lets honest embeds like comments, chat and video logins keep working while browsers block tracking by default. It is also the place where ad and tracking firms ask for access.

use_cases.example: A comment box from another service asks to use your login so you can post.
An embedded video player asks for access so it can keep your login and settings.
A document or design tool embedded in another site asks for its cookies to open your file.
A work app embedded inside another app asks for access so you stay signed in.
A payment frame asks for access to recognise a returning buyer.
An ad or tracking company asks for access, and the browser decides whether to allow it.
A support chat widget asks for access to keep your chat across pages.

technical_bounds: Needs user interaction with the frame first
Denied if the person never visited the embedded site as first party (Firefox: in 30 days)
Cross-site storage not granted for other frames

A store tests cookies and storage before it builds your cart, and shows a warning if they are off.
A fraud service notes that a browser says it supports old Internet Explorer storage tricks, which is a sign of a faked identity.
A fingerprint script builds a profile from which storage tools work and which fail.
A site checks if storage works so it can choose between cookies and a fallback for counting visits.
A web app falls back to a server copy if local storage is off.

capabilities.name: Storage partitioning
capabilities.plain: Browsers key embedded storage by the top site so a tracker sees a separate store on each site.
capabilities.meaning: Cuts the main cross-site tracking path: a widget on site A and site B no longer shares one cookie or localStorage. Embeds can still track within one site, and workarounds shift to link decoration, redirects and server side IDs.

marketing.name: State partitioning
marketing.pitch: Mozilla explains how Firefox splits stored data by the top site to stop cross site tracking.

marketing.name: Tracking Prevention
marketing.pitch: Apple describes how Safari limits cross site tracking, including how embedded storage is isolated.

story.for_you: You get this for free. A tracker or like button embedded on two sites can no longer recognise you as the same person using its own stored data.
story.for_makers: It is a big win for privacy and a loss for old style cross site tracking. Ad firms must move to other signals. Honest embeds, like logins and chat, may need to ask for access.

use_cases.example: An ad network embedded on two news sites sees two different, unlinked visitors instead of one person.
A like or share button on a blog can no longer use its own cookie to see which other sites you visit.
An embedded video player forgets your login on each site until it asks for access.
A support chat widget on a company site keeps a chat only for that site, not across the web.
A game portal that embeds each game keeps game saves apart per portal.
A measurement firm can no longer follow a visitor across client sites using embedded storage.
A fraud service embedded on many sites loses a shared ID and must use other signals.

Includes cookies (Firefox, Safari), localStorage, IndexedDB, Cache, BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker
Chrome partitions storage but keeps unpartitioned cookies as a user choice

Total Cookie Protection by default for all users

marketing.name: Storage for the web
marketing.pitch: Google explains how much a site can store and how browsers manage quota and cleanup.

story.for_you: You never see the limit, until a site runs out of room. Then it may stop saving, ask you to free space or lose offline data.
story.for_makers: Makers plan their offline features around the limit. A big game or editor needs lots of space. The quota number and the way it behaves can also help tell browsers and private modes apart.

use_cases.example: A browser game with large levels checks the quota first, then downloads only what fits.
A podcast or music web app tells you how many songs it can keep offline.
A web video editor warns you before a project grows beyond the space it can store.
A web email app keeps the last month of mail offline, as much as the quota allows.
A fraud service notes a tiny quota, which can mean private mode or an emulator.
A site team measures typical quotas to design offline features.
A fingerprint script reads the exact quota number as one more clue about your device and disk.

marketing.name: Page Lifecycle API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes events that tell a page when the browser freezes or discards it to save memory.

marketing.name: Back/forward cache
marketing.pitch: Google says bfcache makes the Back button instant by keeping a whole page in memory.

story.for_you: You see it as an instant Back button, and tabs that come back right where you left them. Behind the scenes the page is frozen when hidden and woken up when you return.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to save your work before a tab is frozen and to make the Back button feel instant, which helps sales and speed scores. It also lets ad and analytics scripts know when to send their last report.

use_cases.example: You press Back from a product page and the search results appear instantly with your scroll position.
A web editor saves your draft the moment the tab is frozen, so nothing is lost.
A browser game pauses and keeps its state when the tab is frozen, then restores it when you return.
An analytics script sends its last data when the page is hidden, since the unload event is not reliable.
A video site remembers your playback spot when the tab is discarded and reloaded.
A chat app reconnects and catches up on messages when a tab is restored from the cache.
A news site refreshes stale content when a cached page is restored, so you do not read old headlines.

unload handlers block bfcache in several browsers; Chrome has been phasing unload out gradually (check current status)
Chrome discards background tabs under memory pressure; the time before freeze is not fixed
beacon via visibilitychange is the reliable last chance to send data

Sending data as the tab hides

history.change: Desktop back/forward cache enabled for most users

marketing.name: Reporting API
marketing.pitch: Describes a standard way for browsers to send reports about problems to a site's chosen endpoint.

story.for_makers: Teams use it to catch crashes and blocked content from real visitors, which a test lab would miss. It also helps teams roll out stronger security rules safely, in report only mode first.

use_cases.example: A bank turns on a strict content policy in report mode and learns which scripts it would block before it enforces.
A browser game studio gets crash reports from real players on rare phones.
A site learns that a feature it uses will be removed in the next browser, and plans a fix.
A retailer sees reports that a third party script is being blocked, and finds a broken checkout step.

A news site uses reports about intervention warnings to stop heavy ads that freeze the page.

marketing.name: requestAnimationFrame
marketing.pitch: Tells the browser to run animation code just before the next screen refresh, for smooth motion.

story.for_you: You never see a prompt. It is why animations and games look smooth. When you switch tabs, the browser pauses it to save power. It also shows how fast your screen refreshes.
story.for_makers: It is the heartbeat of every browser game and animation. It lets code draw in time with the screen and pause when hidden. The timing also reveals the refresh rate, which is a small device clue.

use_cases.example: A browser game like Krunker.io calls it every frame to move players and draw the scene.
A design tool redraws only when needed, in step with the screen, so panning stays smooth.
A web map redraws tiles and labels in each frame while you drag.
A video player draws overlays like subtitles in time with each frame.
An ad script uses frame timing to check the ad was truly on screen and not hidden in a background tab.
A bot detector sees that frames never run, a sign of a hidden or headless browser.

A site wakes in the background to send queued usage data it could not send before.
A bank wakes on push to show a login approval prompt.

story.for_makers: Trackers moved to redirects when third party cookies got blocked. Browsers answered by deleting data from sites you did not really visit. Makers of login or payment redirects must make sure that real people interact with their site, or it may be treated as a tracker.

A link shortener passes you through its domain to count clicks. Safari and Chrome may erase its cookie.
A game login that bounces you through a different account site must get a click there, or your session data may be cleared.
A shared link wrapper on a social site that redirects to the target may lose its cookie if people never interact with it.

story.for_makers: A site that sells or shares data must honor opt outs, or face fines per violation. Ad companies now add checks for signals like GPC and state laws. Makers also need to keep records and teach teams to turn tags off when a visitor opts out.

A news site with ads uses a consent tool that applies the California rules by location.

Not a technical control

marketing.name: CHIPS
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes it as a way for embedded services to keep cookies that are split per top level site.

story.for_you: You do not see it. A chat box, map or payment widget on a site can remember you on that site only. It cannot use the same cookie to know you on another site.
story.for_makers: Widgets still need to remember state, like a chat session or a login, after third party cookies went away. Splitting the cookie per site gives them that without a cross site profile. The 10 KiB cap makes it hard to store much.

An embedded game on a portal saves your progress for that portal only, and does not follow you to other portals.
A bot checking widget keeps a short session on each site separately, which stops it from building a cross site list of visitors.

A news site sets up a tag server on its domain, so its ad partners can set cookies as though they were the site.
A game portal hides its ad partner behind a subdomain so ads and player tracking are not blocked.
A privacy researcher uses DNS lookups to spot a hidden tracker behind a friendly sounding subdomain.

story.for_makers: Real time ad auctions need every bidder to know who is on the page. Syncing lets them match their private IDs with each other. The result is a web of IDs that makes ads follow people, and a large share of sites take part.

use_cases.example: A news page loads, and a dozen ad companies swap IDs so they can bid on you within 100 milliseconds.
A measurement company uses synced IDs to count people who saw an ad on one site and bought on another.

marketing.pitch: Chrome pitched it as a way for sites of one organization to share cookies in limited, declared groups.

story.for_you: You never saw it. A company could list its own sites as one group. The browser would then let them share cookies without a prompt. It was retired in 2025.
story.for_makers: Big brands with many domains wanted to keep login across them. The list was a small fix to cookie blocking. It also let a company decide who counted as the same owner, which worried privacy groups.

use_cases.example: A news company with several sites kept one login across them.
A retailer shared a cart across its brand sites.
A game company shared login across its store, forums and game sites.
A social network used the group for one sign in across its apps.
An ad network could have shown the same ad profile across sites of one brand.
A software firm shared session cookies among its app and help domains.

technical_bounds: Primary site plus max 5 associated sites
Needed a public GitHub submission
Only Chrome ever shipped

abuse: Cross-site cookie sharing between a company's domains

history.change: Retirement announced including requestStorageAccessFor and Related Website Partition
Removal postponed to Chrome 152 (post dated Jun 10 2026)
requestStorageAccessFor approved for removal in 153; code removal in 154 to 155

web.api: Meta Pixel fbq('track', ...), Google tag gtag('event', ...), LinkedIn Insight Tag, server APIs

access.persistence: Membership windows set per audience: Meta up to 180 days, Google Ads up to 540 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can add you to an ad list when you visit a site, so ads follow you
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit a site with an ad pixel
can: Add you to a list tied to your visit
Let the site owner target you with ads on other platforms
Use pages you viewed or items you added to a cart as the trigger

limits.differs: Safari and Firefox limit pixel cookies. Chrome allows them.

story.what_it_is: Ad pixels add you to lists so the site's owner can show you ads elsewhere.

marketing.name: Custom Audiences
marketing.pitch: Meta pitches it as a way to reach people who visited your site or are in your lists with ads.

story.for_you: You look at a product, then see that product in ads for days. A pixel put you in a list. The list can last 180 days on Meta and 540 on Google Ads.
story.for_makers: People who already showed interest buy more often than strangers. Retargeting lists turn visits into a cheap ad audience. They are one of the main reasons sites run ad pixels.

use_cases.example: You leave a pair of shoes in the cart and see them on Instagram all week.
Google remarketing follows you with display ads for the same product for weeks.
A game website retargets people who visited the store page but did not buy, with a sale ad.
You search for flights, and ads for that route follow you around.
A software firm shows case studies to people who visited the pricing page.
A subscription site shows you a deal after you hit its paywall.

risks: Based on pages you thought were private

technical_bounds: Platforms require minimum audience sizes before serving (about 100 to 1000 matched users, varies by product)
Needs the person to be recognisable (cookie, click ID or hashed email)
Consent rules (GDPR, ePrivacy) apply to the tags in the EU

abuse: Following a person across sites and apps after a single visit

linkedin.how: LinkedIn Insight Tag and its ad stack use this technique on advertiser sites (see research/linkedin-case.md).

history.change: Google Consent Mode v2 required for EEA remarketing audiences
Privacy Sandbox Protected Audience, the in-browser retargeting alternative, retired

capabilities.name: Safari 27 IP based tracker blocking (beta)
capabilities.plain: Safari 27 beta checks the server IP of outgoing requests and can block known ad tracker ranges.
capabilities.meaning: Per a July 2026 code review, Safari 27 beta blocks connections by destination IP (found for bat.bing.com) and puts LinkedIn Insight (snap.licdn.com) on the fingerprinting list so it loses query and referrer data. Unverified beyond one secondary report.

web.api: Browser feature, no site API; blocks request at network layer

access.persistence: Rules in a system library Apple can update without a Safari release
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can block requests to known ad tracker servers by their IP address in Safari 27 beta
limits.user_action: Nothing. Safari 27 does it on its own while you browse
can: Check the server address of outgoing requests
Block requests to known ad tracker address ranges
Work even when a tracker hides behind a different name
cannot: Run in Chrome, Edge or Firefox
Run in Safari before version 27, or outside the beta for now
Block trackers that share an address with normal sites
Stop first party tracking by the site itself
limits.differs: Only Safari 27 beta on Mac and iPhone does this. Other browsers do not.

story.what_it_is: Safari 27 beta may block ad trackers by their server address. Reported, not fully confirmed.
story.for_you: You would never see it. In the beta, Safari may stop connecting to known ad tracker server addresses, and strip data from LinkedIn's tracker. Fewer tracking calls would go out from your browser.
story.for_makers: Blocking by address beats disguises like CNAME cloaking. Advertisers using Bing or LinkedIn tags could lose measurement in Safari. This is based on one secondary report, so it may change.

use_cases.example: An advertiser loses sales data from Safari users, because the Bing tag cannot connect.
A marketer sees a drop in LinkedIn tracked visits from iPhones.
A shop sees fewer retargeting events from Safari shoppers.
A game ad campaign gets lower counts of installs credited to Bing ads from Safari users.
A researcher reads the Safari code to find which tracker addresses are on the list.
A publisher with tracker tags sees less data from Safari readers.

technical_bounds: Server side tagging is unaffected because the browser never calls the tracker
First party proxying does not help because destination IPs stay the same
Stable release date not announced as of Jul 2026

linkedin.how: LinkedIn Insight Tag (snap.licdn.com) is on Safari's fingerprinting classification list per the July 2026 review.

history.change: TAGGRS analysis of WebKit source (Jul 6 2026): IP checks, LinkedIn Insight on fingerprint list

capabilities.name: Safari 7 day script storage deletion
capabilities.plain: Safari deletes a site's script written storage after 7 days of Safari use without a visit to the site.
capabilities.meaning: Covers localStorage, IndexedDB, Cache, service workers, media keys and script set cookies. The counter is days of Safari use, not calendar days. Installed Home Screen web apps are exempt. Limits long lived tracker storage.

access.persistence: Deleted when Safari use passes 7 days with no user interaction on the site
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can't keep script saved data in Safari after 7 days of use without a visit
limits.user_action: Nothing. Safari does it for you in the background.
can: Keep data for as long as you visit the site at least once every 7 days of Safari use
Keep data when it is added to your Home screen as an app
Keep cookies set by the site's server, as opposed to its scripts
cannot: Keep script saved data, such as localStorage, IndexedDB and cookies set by scripts, after 7 days of Safari use without a visit
Get around the limit by asking Safari
Be affected the same way in Chrome or Firefox
limits.differs: Safari on iPhone and Mac only. Chrome and Firefox do not do this.

story.what_it_is: Safari erases a site's script stored data if you skip the site for 7 days of Safari use.

marketing.name: Full third party cookie blocking and more
marketing.pitch: Apple announced Safari limits on script written storage as part of its work against cross site tracking.

marketing.name: Tracking Prevention
marketing.pitch: Apple describes Safari's tracking protections, including how long some site data lives.

story.for_you: If you do not visit a site for a week of Safari use, it may forget you. You might have to log in again or lose a saved score or setting.
story.for_makers: It shortens the life of trackers that hide IDs in storage. It also cuts the life of honest sites, so makers rely on server side cookies or ask people to install the web app to avoid it.

use_cases.example: A tracker that kept a visitor ID in local storage loses it after a week away, so Safari users look new on return.
A casual browser game loses a local save if you skip a couple of weeks, unless you sign in or install it.
A store forgets your wishlist stored in the browser if you do not come back soon.
A measurement team sees Safari visitors counted as new more often, because the ID expired.
A note app on Safari asks you to sign in or install it so offline notes are not removed.
A news site loses your reading list kept in local storage after a week away.

technical_bounds: Counts days Safari was used
Home Screen web apps have no cap
Server set first party cookies are not covered unless cloaked or IP mismatched
Interaction (tap or click) resets the clock

history.change: 7 day cap on all script writable storage

refs.label: WebKit: Full third party cookie blocking and more

capabilities.name: Search engine referral data loss
capabilities.plain: Search engines no longer pass the search keywords to the site; only the engine name arrives.
capabilities.meaning: Since Oct 2011 Google withholds queries for signed in then all searches ('not provided'). Sites see the origin google.com only and learn keywords through Search Console (up to 1000 rows per query export) or on site search.

access.persistence: Per visit
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can't see the search words you used, only the search engine's name
limits.user_action: You click a result on a search engine
can: Tell that you came from a search engine
Know which engine you used
Use other tools to learn which words bring visitors
cannot: See your search words from most engines
Tell which result you saw
Link your search to a personal profile
See keywords unless the site has search console data or paid ad data

story.what_it_is: Search engines stopped sending the words you searched to the sites you visit.

marketing.name: Search Console
marketing.pitch: Google points sites to Search Console for search query data, in place of per visit keywords.

story.for_you: You search and click a result. The site learns you came from Google, but not what you typed. That keeps your search private from the site.
story.for_makers: Sites lost the exact words visitors used, which they once saw in analytics. They now get grouped query data from Search Console, or learn from their own site search. It changed how SEO teams work.

use_cases.example: A blog owner sees most traffic as Google, with the term not provided, and uses Search Console to guess topics.
A shop uses its own on site search to see what people want, since Google keeps the words.
A news site sees which stories rise on Google through Search Console clicks.
A game site learns top search words from Search Console and builds pages for them.
Paid search ads still get keyword data, which is why ad clicks are better tracked.
A school sees only that a student came from Google, not which question they asked.

risks: Sites guess at what you wanted
Paid ads still see more data

technical_bounds: Query not in Referer or document.referrer
Search Console data limited to 16 months and sampled to top queries
AI chat referrers often send only utm_source such as chatgpt.com

abuse: Scraping query terms from legacy referrers on HTTP

history.change: Google starts encrypting searches; keyword data becomes 'not provided'
Default referrer policy trims all cross-origin referrers to origin

capabilities.name: navigator.sendBeacon
capabilities.plain: Sends a small POST that the browser delivers even while the person is leaving the page.
capabilities.meaning: Lets analytics report time on page, scroll depth and exit clicks after the tab is closed or navigated away. No response is readable. The person cannot see or stop it, and it carries cookies for the target origin.

access.persistence: Fire and forget; queued by the browser until sent
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can send a small report that the browser delivers even as you leave the page
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you close or leave a page
can: Send a small message as the page closes
Report time spent, clicks or errors
Deliver the message even after the tab is gone
cannot: Send large amounts of data, since there is a size limit
Get a reply back to the page
Run if a blocker stops the request
Show a prompt or any sign
limits.reach_label: A last report, as you leave

story.what_it_is: Sends a small message that the browser delivers even as you leave the page.

marketing.name: sendBeacon
marketing.pitch: Developer docs describe it as a way to send a small amount of data in the background, even on page exit.

story.for_you: You never see it. You close a tab or click away, and the page sends a last note that gets delivered. You cannot read it, stop it or know what it held.
story.for_makers: Normal requests are cut off when a page closes. sendBeacon lets analytics finish a report about time on page, scrolls or exits. It is simple, so it is everywhere.

use_cases.example: A news site sends how long you read and how far you scrolled when you leave the article.
A browser game sends final stats when you close the tab, so the server records your run.
A video site sends your watch time so it can resume next visit.
An ad tag reports that an ad was seen for 2 seconds.
A fraud tool sends last mouse and key data on exit from a checkout page.
An app sends crash and speed data as the tab closes.

risks: Carries cookies to the target site

technical_bounds: About 64 KiB of queued beacon and keepalive data per page (Chrome)
POST only, response not readable
Returns false if the data is refused
Blocked by tracker blockers

abuse: Post-visit tracking that survives page close

capabilities.name: Server side tagging
capabilities.plain: The site sends its analytics to its own server first, which relays it to ad vendors.
capabilities.meaning: Moves tracking from the browser to the site's cloud container, so blockers cannot see vendor calls and cookies are set by the site's own server. The vendor can still receive IP, user agent, hashed email and click IDs the server chooses to forward.

web.api: Google Tag Manager server container on a first party subdomain; Set-Cookie from server

access.persistence: Server set cookies can last up to 400 days but Safari caps IP mismatched ones at 7 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can send your activity to the site's own server first, then on to ad vendors
limits.user_action: Nothing on your side. It happens as you use a site that routes data through its server
can: Collect your visits on the site's own server
Pass them to ad and analytics vendors
Choose what data each vendor receives, including fewer details
cannot: Be seen or blocked by your browser, since the relay is out of sight
Add details the browser never sent
Work unless the site has set it up
Give vendors your data if the site chooses not to pass it on
limits.reach_label: What the site chooses to pass on

story.what_it_is: A site sends its tracking to its own server first, which passes it on to ad vendors.

marketing.name: Server side tagging
marketing.pitch: Google pitches it as moving tags to a server container for faster pages, more control and better data.

story.for_you: You never see it. Instead of loading many vendor scripts, the page sends one stream to the site's own server. Blockers cannot see vendor calls, and cookies are set by the site's own server.
story.for_makers: Pages load faster and the company controls what each vendor gets. It also gets around blockers and short cookie limits. The server can still forward IP, hashed email and click IDs.

use_cases.example: A shop sends all events to its own server, then to Google Analytics and Meta, so pages load faster.
An advertiser sets a first party cookie from its own server, so it lasts longer than a script cookie.
A game store sends purchase events through its server to ad networks, with no vendor script on the page.
A publisher removes dozens of ad scripts from the page and sends data from its server.
A company hashes email on its server and drops IP before sharing, to cut what vendors see.
A retailer adds server events to fill gaps when shoppers use blockers.

risks: Cannot be blocked in your browser
Company decides what each vendor sees

technical_bounds: Server must forward data on its own authority
Consent rules still apply
Safari caps cookies from servers on different IP ranges
Browser mitigations like Safari 27 IP blocking do not see server to server calls

abuse: Evading blockers, covert hashed email forwarding

capabilities.name: Service worker lifetime
capabilities.plain: A background script registered by a site that persists after the tab is closed.
capabilities.meaning: It can intercept every request, serve cached content, and wake for push or sync even when no page is open. The browser stops it after about 30 seconds idle, but the registration stays until cleared. Safari deletes it after 7 days of non use.

access.persistence: Registration persists with no fixed expiry. Script checked for update at most every 24 hours. Idle stop after about 30 s (Chrome)
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can keep a background helper script for a site that stays after you close the tab
limits.user_action: Nothing. It is set up the first time you visit a site that uses one
can: Intercept the site's own requests and serve saved copies
Wake for push or sync when you allow them
Keep the helper registered until you clear it or the site removes it
Make a site load fast and work offline
cannot: See other sites' requests or data, since it is limited to the one site
Stay running, as the browser stops it after about 30 seconds idle
Last in Safari beyond 7 days without a visit
Survive when you clear that site's data
limits.differs: Safari deletes a site's helper after 7 days without use. Chrome, Edge and Firefox keep it until cleared.

story.what_it_is: A background script a site installs, which stays on your device after you close the tab.

marketing.name: Tracking prevention
marketing.pitch: Safari limits how long background scripts and site data can live for sites you do not use.

story.for_you: You never see it. A site you visited can leave a small helper that makes it load faster and work offline. It can also stay around for a long time unless the browser clears it.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for offline, caching, push and fast loads. It acts like a tiny server on your device. It can also keep an identity link or run tracking code, so browsers limit its lifetime.

use_cases.example: A news site caches pages so you can read offline on a plane.
A browser game caches its files, so it starts in a second the next time and works offline.
A web editor like Google Docs keeps its code locally so it opens fast and works offline.
A store caches its catalog so browsing feels instant on a weak signal.
An ad or tracking script installs a helper to survive cookie clearing and measure visits later.
A web chat uses a helper to receive push messages when the tab is closed.
A malicious site installs a helper that keeps showing spam alerts after you leave.

technical_bounds: Idle termination about 30 s, single event up to about 5 min (Chrome)
HTTPS only
Same origin scope
Safari 7 day cap on registrations without user visit
Cleared by Clear site data

abuse: Persistent hidden request interception, tracker caching

history.change: ITP 7 day storage cap covers registrations

capabilities.name: Session replay
capabilities.plain: A script records page changes, mouse, scroll and typing so staff can replay a visit like a video.
capabilities.meaning: Shows exactly what the person saw and did, including text typed in forms unless masked. A 2017 Princeton study found replay scripts on 482 of the top 50,000 sites leaking data. In 2022 to 2025 US wiretap suits grew.

web.api: MutationObserver, mouse, scroll and input event listeners sending to vendor

access.persistence: Vendor retention often 30 days to 13 months
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can record your clicks, scrolls and typing on a page so staff can replay it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you use a page with a replay script
can: Record page changes, mouse moves, clicks and scrolls
Record what you type, unless fields are masked
Let staff replay your visit like a video
cannot: Record other sites, tabs or apps
Show fields the site has masked, such as passwords and card numbers
Work if a tracker blocker stops the script
Name you unless the site links it to a login
limits.reach_label: Your whole visit on that site

story.what_it_is: A script records your mouse, clicks and typing so staff can replay your visit like a video.
story.for_you: You never see it. While you use a site, a script records page changes, mouse, scroll and keys. Staff may later watch your visit. It can capture text you type unless the site masks it.
story.for_makers: Teams watch real visits to find bugs and confusing screens. Replay shows what a person saw. It has also brought privacy suits, because replay scripts can capture personal data.

use_cases.example: A shop watches a replay of a checkout that failed, and finds a button that did not work on phones.
A browser game studio replays a stuck player session to find a bug in the menu.
An engineer watches the last 30 seconds before a crash to reproduce a bug.
A bank watches how people fill a loan form, with the number fields masked.
A support team opens a replay of a customer's session to see what went wrong.
A fraud team watches replay for a login session that looks scripted.

technical_bounds: Masks password and payment fields by default in most tools
Needs vendor script on page (blocked by many tools)
Cross-origin iframes need their own script
Consent required in EU and under California wiretap suits

abuse: Capturing typed text, emails and health data

history.change: Princeton: 482 of the top 50,000 sites used replay scripts

refs.label: No boundaries: session replay scripts (Freedom to Tinker 2017)

capabilities.name: Shared Storage API (retired)
capabilities.plain: Cross-site storage whose values could only be read in a locked worker. Retired Oct 2025.
capabilities.meaning: Let scripts write cross-site values (for example a frequency count) and read them only inside a worklet that output through limited channels (selectURL, Private Aggregation). Disabled starting build 153.0.8001.0; code removal follows.

access.persistence: Entries expire after 30 days, renewable on write
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

data.metric: Key/value pairs readable in worklet only

limits.headline: Can't store cross site data for ads in Chrome anymore, since it was retired in 2025
limits.user_action: Nothing. It used to happen in the background on pages with embedded ads
can: Have stored values in the browser that any site could use through a locked worker
Have helped choose an ad or count reach without naming you
cannot: Run in Chrome after retirement
Work in Edge, Firefox or Safari
Show stored values to the page directly
Replace cookies for all ad needs

story.what_it_is: Chrome storage that held cross site values in a locked room. Retired.

marketing.name: Shared Storage API
marketing.pitch: Chrome pitched it as unpartitioned storage that could be read only in a locked worklet with limited outputs.

story.for_you: You never saw it. A script could write a value, such as a count, that other sites could read only inside a locked worker. Chrome is turning it off. You will not meet it.
story.for_makers: It was meant to help with things like frequency capping and A/B tests without tracking. Reads had to go through limited paths. With the Privacy Sandbox ad parts retired, it is going away.

use_cases.example: An ad network counted how many times you saw an ad across sites to avoid showing it too often.
A test tool used it to keep the same A or B design across sites you visit.
A game studio could cap how often it showed the same promo across sites.
A publisher used it to pick which ad creative to show without a profile.
A retailer used it to know a visitor saw a sale ad on a partner site.
A social login widget could have stored a flag across sites, read only in a safe room.

selectURL leaks log2(n) bits capped at about 12 bits per 24 hours per top-level site (budget)
No direct script access to values
Chrome only
