capabilities.name: Speculation Rules prefetch and prerender
capabilities.plain: A page can load a likely next page early, so a site may see a request before the person visits.
capabilities.meaning: Prefetch or prerender makes the destination server log a hit, and run scripts, before any click, sending Sec-Purpose: prefetch;prerender. Analytics can over count; cookies from a prefetched response apply only on activation.

access.persistence: Prefetch cache about 5 minutes in Chrome
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

safari.note: Not supported at time of research, verify

limits.headline: Can load a likely next page early, so a site may see a visit first
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page guesses where you will go next
can: Load a likely next page before you click
Show the next page almost instantly when you click
Let the next site see a request before you visit
cannot: Run in Firefox or Safari
Run when Chrome's data saver is on or the connection is poor
Show you the page until you click, or count it as a visit in some tools
Load pages from a different site without extra signals
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet support it. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: A page can load a likely next page early, so a site may see a visit before you click.

marketing.name: Prerender pages
marketing.pitch: Chrome says speculation rules can load pages ahead of time so the next click feels instant.

story.for_you: You click a link and the next page appears almost at once. Behind the scenes, the browser loaded it before you clicked. The site may log a hit even if you never open it.
story.for_makers: Instant page loads raise sales and reading time. But prefetching makes the server count a visit early and can run scripts before you arrive. Analytics must wait for activation to avoid inflated numbers.

use_cases.example: A shop prerenders the product page you are likely to open, so checkout feels fast.
A news site prefetches the next article so it opens instantly.
A game portal prefetches the page of the game you hover over, so it loads in a blink.
A tool must ignore hits from prefetched pages, or visit counts go up.
An ad system waits for activation before it counts an impression.
A search result page prerenders the top result so it opens at once.

risks: Server sees visits you never made

technical_bounds: Same-site prefetch carries cookies; cross-origin uses an isolated session without them
Not done when Data Saver or Save-Data is on, or in low memory
Chrome limits concurrent prefetch and prerender counts

abuse: Phantom page views, privacy leak of intent before click

history.change: Prerender2 shipped for omnibox and speculation rules

capabilities.name: Storage Access API
capabilities.plain: Lets an embedded frame ask to use its third-party cookies; the browser may prompt or auto-allow.
capabilities.meaning: Used by embedded SSO, comments and video frames to regain cross-site cookies on Safari, Firefox and Chrome. Safari prompts per embed; Firefox auto-grants after 5 prior interactions and a prompt in other cases; Chrome shows a prompt.

access.prompt_ui: Browser prompt: allow site to use cookies and data on this site
access.persistence: Chrome grant lasts 30 days for the embed; Safari 24 hours of use then reprompt (approx.); Firefox 30 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings
access.iframe: Granted per embedded frame; sandbox needs allow-storage-access-by-user-activation

limits.user_action: You click a button in an embed, such as a login or comment box, and see a prompt
can: Ask the browser to let an embedded frame use its own cookies
Keep you signed in to that embedded service
Get approved without a prompt in some cases, based on past use
cannot: Use the cookies without approval from the browser or you
Reach cookies of other sites
Work if you click Don't allow
Persist forever, since browsers can ask again
limits.differs: Safari and Firefox show a prompt or approve automatically after use. Chrome allows it with less friction.

story.what_it_is: Lets an embedded frame ask to use its cookies from other sites, and the browser may prompt you.

marketing.name: Storage Access API
marketing.pitch: WebKit introduced it as a way for embedded content to ask for cookie access with the person's consent.

story.for_you: You see a prompt in some browsers: this site wants to use cookies on another site. If you allow it, an embedded login, comment box or video frame can recognise you. In some browsers, it grants after some use.
story.for_makers: Single sign on, comments and paid video frames need cookies from their own domain. The API gives them a way back in after blocking. It also gives the browser a place to ask the person, as a check on trackers.

use_cases.example: A comment box from a social site recognises you inside a news article, and lets you post.
A paid video embed checks your subscription cookie from its own domain, so it can play for you.
A game inside a portal frame uses its cookie to remember your login and progress.
A work tool embedded in another app uses its login cookie in the frame.
A payment frame recognises your saved card details, from its own domain.
Browsers use the prompt to stop trackers hidden in embeds from asking for cookies for free.

risks: Prompt can be clicked without thinking

technical_bounds: Needs a user gesture in the iframe
Frame must have interacted as first party in the past (Safari, Firefox)
Sandboxed frames need allow-storage-access-by-user-activation

abuse: Embedded tracker regaining cookies after prompt fatigue

capabilities.name: IAB TCF consent string
capabilities.plain: A coded record of which ad vendors and purposes the person agreed to in the EU consent banner.
capabilities.meaning: Stored in the euconsent-v2 cookie and read through __tcfapi. TCF v2.3 requires the disclosedVendors segment, and strings without it were invalid from Feb 28 2026. Consent is valid for up to 13 months.

access.persistence: euconsent-v2 cookie up to 13 months
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can see which ad vendors you agreed to in the EU cookie banner
limits.user_action: You tap Accept, Reject, or Manage choices on a cookie banner
can: Check which ad vendors and purposes you said yes to
Pass your choices along to the ad partners it works with
Remember your answer for up to 13 months
Show the banner again if the record is missing or out of date
cannot: Count a choice you never made as your consent
Use a record that lacks the vendor list; since Feb 28 2026 those strings are invalid
Keep your choices past 13 months without asking again
Tell vendors you agreed when you picked Reject all
limits.reach_label: Only choices you made in the banner

story.what_it_is: A saved note of which ad companies and purposes you said yes or no to on a cookie banner.

marketing.name: Transparency and Consent Framework
marketing.pitch: The industry standard that lets sites, ad vendors and consent banners share one record of what a person agreed to.

story.for_you: You see it as the cookie banner in Europe, with a button to accept, reject or manage choices. After you tap, the site stores a coded note of your answers. Ad companies on the page read that note instead of asking you again.
story.for_makers: Publishers and ad vendors need proof that a person agreed before personal data is used for ads. The string travels with every ad request, so each buyer knows what it may do. It also keeps a paper trail for regulators.

use_cases.example: A European newspaper shows a banner, then passes your choices to every ad vendor on the page so only allowed ones load.
In a real-time ad auction, the exchange reads the string first and drops bidders that were not approved.
A free browser games portal shows a consent banner on first visit and only runs personalised ads between rounds if you agreed.
A streaming site plays a generic pre-roll ad instead of a targeted one when you reject the banner.
A measurement tag waits for the consent note before it fires, so rejected visitors are not counted individually.
A web shop only loads retargeting pixels from vendors you ticked, so you do not see its ads follow you around.
A compliance team keeps logs of consent strings to show a regulator that a visitor really said yes.

risks: Consent claims that regulators have challenged

technical_bounds: Covers 11 purposes and 3 special purposes plus vendor IDs
Needs a registered CMP
Not a legal proof by itself

abuse: Weak consent flows (CNIL and Belgian DPA rulings on TCF)

history.change: TCF v2.2 removed legitimate interest for some purposes
TCF v2.3 with disclosedVendors mandatory from Feb 28 2026

capabilities.name: Third-party cookies by browser (Nov 2026)
capabilities.plain: Whether an embedded site can set and read its own cookies on other sites, which varies by browser.
capabilities.meaning: Third-party cookies are how ad networks recognise the same person across sites. Safari blocks them, Firefox partitions them, Brave blocks them, Chrome leaves them on by default (user choice) and blocks them in Incognito.

web.api: document.cookie in iframes; Set-Cookie with SameSite=None; Secure; Storage Access API

access.persistence: Cookie lifetime per cookie; Chrome caps at 400 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

chrome.note: 3PC allowed by default; blocked in Incognito

samsung.note: Allowed by default, Smart Anti-Tracking blocks some

data.metric: Cookie jar per top-level site (partitioned) or global

limits.headline: Can recognise you across sites with embedded cookies, unless your browser blocks them
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page with ads or embeds loads
can: Set and later see its own cookie from inside a page on another site
Link your visits across the sites that embed it
Keep working in Chrome, where these cookies stay on by default
Ask the browser for access if it was blocked (Storage Access prompt)
cannot: Set these cookies in Safari, which blocks them
Share one cookie across sites in Firefox, which keeps a separate jar per site
Use them in Incognito windows in Chrome
Get through in Brave, which blocks them
limits.differs: Safari and Brave block them, Firefox splits them per site, and Chrome allows them by default but blocks them in Incognito.

story.what_it_is: Whether an embedded site can store cookies on other sites, which depends on which browser you use.

marketing.name: Intelligent Tracking Prevention
marketing.pitch: Safari blocks cross-site tracking by default so websites cannot follow you from site to site.

marketing.name: Enhanced Tracking Protection
marketing.pitch: Firefox keeps each site's cookies in a separate jar so trackers cannot connect your visits.

marketing.name: Privacy Sandbox
marketing.pitch: Chrome kept third-party cookies and gives people a choice, while offering newer ad tools as alternatives.

story.for_you: You never see these cookies, but they decide whether an ad for boots follows you from a shoe shop to a news site. In Safari and Firefox it mostly cannot. In Chrome it still can, unless you turn it off in settings.
story.for_makers: Ad networks use these cookies to recognise the same person across sites for targeting, frequency caps and conversion counting. Sites also use them for legitimate embeds like logins and payments. When a browser blocks them, makers must switch to first-party data or new APIs.

use_cases.example: A retailer's ad network sets a cookie when you view boots, then recognises you on a recipe blog and shows the same boots.
A Like or Share button embedded on a news article recognises your logged-in account and counts the visit.
An embedded video on a blog remembers your player settings and view history through the video host's own cookie.
A browser game embedded in a portal page saves your progress under the game host's cookie, which breaks when the browser blocks it.
A card check inside a frame on a shop page relies on the bank's cookie to recognise a trusted device.
A bot defence service sets one cookie across many customer sites to spot a scraper hopping between them.
A marketing platform ties an ad click on one site to a purchase on another to report which campaign worked.

risks: Settings differ by browser, so protection is uneven

technical_bounds: Safari: blocked for all, no exceptions except Storage Access API
Firefox: Total Cookie Protection partitions per top-level site by default (June 2022, Firefox 103)
Chrome: kept on by default; no deprecation prompt after the April 2025 decision; Incognito blocks by default
Edge: Tracking Prevention blocks classified trackers, not all

legit_uses: Embedded video, chat, SSO, payment frames
abuse: Cross-site profile building by ad networks

history.change: Total Cookie Protection default for all users
1% of Chrome users had third-party cookies restricted (testing)
Google proposed user choice instead of deprecation
Google confirmed no standalone prompt; users keep the Settings choice
Oct 17: Google retired most remaining Privacy Sandbox APIs; third-party cookies stay

capabilities.name: Topics API (retired)
capabilities.plain: Chrome's interest-topic API for ads. Deprecated in Chrome 144 and being removed in 2026.
capabilities.meaning: Gave ad scripts up to 3 coarse interest topics (one per recent week) from the browsing history of sites that called it. Taxonomy had 469 topics in v2; 5% of results were random noise. Removal rolling out from Chrome 153.

access.persistence: Epoch of 1 week; 3 most recent epochs returned; observed topics kept for 3 weeks
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can't pick your interests from your browsing any more; Chrome is retiring this
limits.user_action: Nothing. It used to run when an ad script loaded in Chrome
can: Still work in some older Chrome versions until removal rolls out from Chrome 153
Hand ad scripts up to 3 broad interest topics, one per recent week
cannot: Run in Safari, Firefox, or Edge
Give exact sites you visited; it shared broad topics only, and 5% were random noise
Keep working after Chrome finishes removing it
Pick topics from sites that never used the feature
limits.differs: Only Chrome ever offered it. Other browsers never did.

story.what_it_is: Chrome's retired feature that told ad scripts a few broad interests, like Sports or Travel.

marketing.name: Topics API
marketing.pitch: Chrome described it as a way to show relevant ads using broad topics instead of tracking you across sites.

story.for_you: You may have seen an Ad topics switch in Chrome settings. Chrome noted a few broad interests from the sites you visit and shared them with ad scripts. This was being removed in 2026, so most people will never meet it.
story.for_makers: Ad companies wanted a replacement for cookies that still let them pick a relevant ad. Topics gave a coarse interest label with no name or ID attached. Few buyers adopted it, which is part of why it was dropped.

use_cases.example: An ad tech script on a news page asks Chrome for your topics and picks a travel ad because Travel was on the list.
A retailer's ad partner favours camping gear ads for visitors whose topics include Outdoors.
A browser games site shows a sports game promo to visitors whose topics include Fitness, without knowing who they are.
A publisher with many logged-out readers lifts ad income by sending topics along with the ad request.
An ad measurement firm compared topic-based ad results with cookie-based results during Chrome's trials.
Ad tech engineers ran Chrome origin trials and tuned their bidding code to use topic labels.

risks: Retired, so old code may linger

technical_bounds: Only returns topics the caller observed on prior sites
5% random topic noise
Up to 3 topics per call, 1 per epoch
Blocked when third-party cookies are off or user disabled Ad topics
Not shipped in Firefox or Safari; Edge disabled it

abuse: Profiling topics across sites by many callers

history.change: Topics shipped with Privacy Sandbox general availability
Oct 17 2025: Google announces retirement of Topics
Removal rollout: 1% stable on 153 and later, paused at 10% until Oct 15 2026, full removal after (per blink-dev as summarised Oct 2 2026)

capabilities.name: UTM campaign parameters
capabilities.plain: Tags in the link URL that tell the site which campaign, medium and source sent the person.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a site tie a visit to a specific ad, email or post. Five standard keys: utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, utm_content. Stored in first-party cookies by analytics tools for the session or longer.

access.persistence: GA4 campaign data is session scoped by default; first-touch copies often kept in cookies for 30 to 90 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can see which ad, email, or post sent you, from tags in the link
limits.user_action: You tap a link that carries campaign tags, such as an ad or email link
can: See the source, medium, and campaign named in the link
Tie your visit to one specific ad, email, or post
Keep that tag in its own cookie for the visit or longer
Count how many people came from each campaign
cannot: See the tags if the link was copied without them
Learn who you are from the tags alone
Follow you to other sites with these tags
Learn what you did before you clicked

story.what_it_is: Little tags added to a link that tell a site which ad, email or post sent you.

marketing.name: Campaign URL builder
marketing.pitch: Google Analytics shows how to add source, medium and campaign tags to links so you can see what drives visits.

story.for_you: You see them as a long tail on a web address, like utm_source=newsletter. Nothing pops up and the page looks the same. The site just learns which link brought you.
story.for_makers: Marketing teams need to know which email, ad or post paid off. The tags are free, work on any site and need no consent banner on their own. They feed dashboards that decide where the next ad budget goes.

use_cases.example: A shoe brand tags each ad so its dashboard shows that the Instagram story brought more buyers than the Google search ad.
A newsletter tags each link so the editor sees which headline readers clicked from the Tuesday email.
A browser game studio tags links on Discord, YouTube and Reddit to learn which place brings players who stay past day one.
A creator adds tags to the link in a bio so a brand can see exactly how many followers visited.
A Black Friday email carries a campaign tag, so the shop ties each order to that email.
A fraud team spots a campaign tag that suddenly brings thousands of fake sign-ups and cuts that source off.
A product team joins the tags with sign-up data to learn which channel brings paying customers.

risks: Links reveal where you came from
Tags can be shared when you copy the link

technical_bounds: Only as accurate as the link author made them
Not stripped by Chrome; Safari and Firefox strip some tracker IDs but leave UTM keys intact
Cannot identify the person alone

abuse: Appending personal data (email, IDs) to links shared widely

history.change: Query Parameter Stripping added for known tracking parameters; UTM keys are not on the strip list
